headline: Bank of Jamaica raises its rate to 6.00%, ending the long hold
stand: The central bank lifted its policy rate 50 basis points to 6.00% on September 28, effective today, in a unanimous vote, its first move after months at 5.50%, as inflation stayed above target for a third straight month. It is the region's benchmark decision, and the signal is that the hold is over.
byline: The Caribbean Ledger, Business and Policy Desk

blocks.x: The Bank of Jamaica raised its policy rate by 50 basis points to 6.00%, a unanimous decision of the Monetary Policy Committee announced on September 28 and effective today. The move ends the long stretch at 5.50% and turns the region's most watched central bank toward tightening (Bank of Jamaica).

Inflation forced the move. Jamaica's August consumer prices rose 7.9% from a year earlier, with core inflation at 5.2%, holding above the four-to-six percent target band for a third consecutive month (STATIN). A central bank that had held its rate through hurricane damage and a soft growth outlook judged that persistent price pressure left no room to wait.

The decision carries beyond Kingston, because it came less than two weeks after the US Federal Reserve raised its own benchmark to a 3.75 to 4.00% range on September 16 in a unanimous 12 to 0 vote (Federal Reserve). With most Caribbean currencies pegged or tightly managed against the US dollar, a higher Fed rate squeezes every regional central bank that wants to avoid a widening gap, and the Bank of Jamaica's turn off the 5.50% hold reads as the region's benchmark answer.

The question now is how far the tightening runs. One 50 basis point step does not make a cycle, but the unanimity of the vote and the third straight month above band suggest the Bank is prepared to move again if inflation does not turn. The Ledger will track the next print and the December policy meeting.

headline: Fidelis Partnership files for a New York listing
stand: The Bermuda-based specialty insurer and reinsurer has filed for an initial public offering on the New York Stock Exchange, a marquee moment for the island's risk-capital hub.

blocks.x: The Fidelis Partnership, the Bermuda-based specialty insurance and reinsurance group, has filed for an initial public offering on the New York Stock Exchange. A completed listing would put one of the island's newer re-insurance names on the region's largest exchange and underline Bermuda's standing as a global center for risk capital.
Pricing, size and timing will come in the prospectus. For Bermuda, the filing is a reminder that the island's core industry still reaches the deepest capital markets in the world (SEC filing).

headline: The Bahamas opens a B$25 million government bond
stand: A new prospectus puts a B$25 million bond in front of domestic investors, part of the routine local financing that funds the budget.

blocks.x: The Bahamas has published a prospectus for a B$25 million government bond, opening the paper to domestic investors as part of its local financing program. It is ordinary budget plumbing rather than a headline raise, but it keeps the government funded through the domestic market rather than in foreign currency (prospectus).

headline: Cayman power disconnections rise 38%
stand: Disconnections by the Caribbean Utilities Company climbed 38%, a cost-of-living signal on an island better known for its wealth.

blocks.x: Disconnections by the Caribbean Utilities Company, Grand Cayman's power provider, rose 38%, a sign that even in one of the region's richest jurisdictions households are feeling the weight of higher bills. The number is a reminder that a high headline income per person can hide real strain underneath (Caribbean Utilities Company).

headline: A Bermuda buyback, and inflation at 2.5%
stand: BAS, a Bermuda-listed company, has opened a share repurchase, while the island's April inflation came in at a mild 2.5%.

blocks.x: BAS, a Bermuda-listed company, has announced a share buyback, returning cash to shareholders. Separately, Bermuda's consumer price index rose 2.5% in April from a year earlier (Bermuda Government, Department of Statistics), a mild reading that stands in contrast to the price pressure driving rate rises elsewhere in the region.

headline: French Guiana and Saint-Martin return their senate results
stand: The overseas French Caribbean voted in France's senatorial elections, a reminder that part of the region sends its representatives to Paris.
byline: The Caribbean Ledger, Politics and Policy Desk

blocks.x: French Guiana and Saint-Martin have returned results in France's senatorial elections, the indirect vote that fills the upper house in Paris. It is a reminder that a slice of the Caribbean is governed as part of France, and that its economic policy is set as much in Europe as in the region (official results).

headline: St. Vincent's borrowing-transparency fight sharpens
stand: A dispute over how fully the government discloses its borrowing has become a live political fight in Kingstown.
byline: The Caribbean Ledger, Politics and Policy Desk

blocks.x: In St. Vincent and the Grenadines, a fight over the transparency of government borrowing has sharpened, with the opposition pressing for fuller disclosure of what the state owes and on what terms. The argument is a small-country version of a universal one: how much a government must show its citizens about the debts taken in their name.

headline: St. Kitts and Nevis re-tenders a Treasury bill
stand: The government returned to the regional market to re-tender a Treasury bill, routine short-term financing at the front end of the curve.

blocks.x: St. Kitts and Nevis has re-tendered a Treasury bill on the Regional Government Securities Market, rolling short-term financing at the front end of its curve. The re-tender is housekeeping rather than news, but it is the kind of steady market access that keeps a small state's finances running (RGSM).

headline: Aeromexico adds a Montego Bay route
stand: The Mexican carrier is opening a route to Montego Bay, widening Jamaica's air links into the Latin American market.

blocks.x: Aeromexico is adding a route to Montego Bay, opening a direct air link between Mexico and Jamaica's second city and its tourism gateway. New lift from a large Latin American carrier widens the funnel of visitors beyond the traditional North American and European markets, and it is the kind of connectivity a tourism economy counts as growth (Aeromexico).

headline: Guyana moves against gold smuggling
stand: A crackdown on gold smuggling aims to keep more of the country's mineral earnings inside the formal economy.

blocks.x: Guyana has launched a crackdown on gold smuggling, moving to keep more of its mineral earnings inside the formal economy. The oil boom has not retired the older extractive sector, and gold remains a meaningful export, so tightening oversight of what leaves the country unrecorded is both a revenue measure and a governance one (Government of Guyana).

headline: Honduras end 13 years without a win over Jamaica, 1-0 in Kingston
stand: Keyrol Figueroa's early goal beat the Reggae Boyz at the National Stadium on September 28, and Honduras held on with ten men. Suriname now top the group, and Jamaica slip to fourth.

blocks.x: Honduras beat Jamaica 1 to 0 at the National Stadium in Kingston on September 28, ending a 13-year run without a win over the Reggae Boyz and denting Jamaica's Concacaf Nations League campaign in League A, Group B. Keyrol Figueroa scored in the 14th minute (Concacaf).

Honduras did it the hard way. They played the final stretch a man down after Denil Moncada was sent off in the 68th minute, and still held the lead to the whistle against a Jamaica side that could not break through at home.

The result reshapes the group. Suriname now top Group B on 6 points, while Jamaica sit fourth on 3. For a Jamaica team carrying regional expectation, a home loss to a side it had not lost to in over a decade is the kind of result that turns a campaign into a question.

headline: Nations League matchday two: Suriname, Curacao, the Dominican Republic and Haiti all win
stand: Around the rest of Concacaf Nations League play, the Caribbean had a strong night, led by a six-goal Curacao and a Haiti shutout of Costa Rica.

blocks.x: Across the second matchday of the Concacaf Nations League, the Caribbean had a strong night. Suriname beat Martinique 2 to 1, Curacao overwhelmed Nicaragua 6 to 1, the Dominican Republic beat Trinidad and Tobago 2 to 1, and Haiti shut out Costa Rica 2 to 0 (Concacaf).

The standouts were Curacao's six-goal display and Haiti's clean sheet against a traditional regional power. Trinidad and Tobago's loss, coming on the same night as Jamaica's, left two of the region's larger footballing nations with work to do in their groups.

headline: Innswood Old Boys win the Rovman Powell T20
stand: Innswood Old Boys took the title in the Twenty20 competition that carries the West Indies captain's name.

blocks.x: Innswood Old Boys won the Rovman Powell T20, the Jamaican club competition that carries the West Indies captain's name. It is the sort of grassroots-to-marquee link that keeps the Caribbean cricket pipeline visible, a local final under a global name (organizers).

headline: Brussels sets a 2028 deadline on Caribbean passports, and the region answers at the UN
stand: The European Commission has told five Eastern Caribbean states to end their citizenship-by-investment programs by June 1, 2028, or lose visa-free access to Europe. At the United Nations, St. Lucia's Philip J. Pierre and Antigua's Gaston Browne carried the region's case to the commissioner in person. They came away with the deadline intact and the harder question unanswered: what replaces the money.

blocks.x: On September 24, in a conference room at the European Union's mission to the United Nations, two Caribbean prime ministers sat across from the man holding a deadline over their economies. Prime Minister Philip J. Pierre of St. Lucia and Prime Minister Gaston Browne of Antigua and Barbuda had come to the 81st General Assembly to make a case that is, at bottom, about money and sovereignty. Across the table was Magnus Brunner, the European commissioner for internal affairs and migration, the official who in June signed the letter giving five Eastern Caribbean states until June 1, 2028 to end the programs that sell their citizenship, or lose the visa-free access to Europe that their passports carry (IMI Daily, The Voice St. Lucia).

They were not alone. Timothy Antoine, the governor of the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, and Didacus Jules, director general of the Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States, sat with them, a signal that the region intends to answer as a bloc rather than as five separate applicants. The prime ministers put the argument plainly, calling the programs an important source of development financing for the OECS countries that operate them, and pressing for a transition path that takes account of both Europe's security concerns and the economic realities of the region. The meeting produced no agreement and no change to the date. The deadline stands.

The instrument behind that deadline is quieter than the headline. On December 30, 2025, a revised European visa-suspension mechanism took force, and for the first time it made the sale of citizenship an independent reason to suspend a country's visa-free travel, in the Commission's words regardless of how well a program is run. On June 25, 2026, Brunner's letter converted that principle into a calendar: a 24-month transition, ending June 1, 2028, for Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, St. Kitts and Nevis, and St. Lucia. The letter also set nearer-term conditions to be met by this month, among them the full exclusion of anyone under EU restrictive measures and reinforced vetting for applicants of every nationality. The next checkpoint is a Commission report due in December.

The reason the region is fighting a date rather than quietly complying sits in the public accounts. For several of these economies, selling citizenship is not a sideline. It is among the largest sources of revenue the state controls, and the cheapest development capital it can raise, with no interest and no lender attached. In Dominica the scale is stark. The International Monetary Fund, in its 2026 Article IV review, put citizenship receipts at roughly 33% of GDP at their 2022 peak, and projected them falling toward 14.5% of GDP by 2030 even before Brussels named a deadline (IMF Staff Country Report No. 2026/117). In St. Kitts and Nevis, the Fund traced part of a 2025 slowdown directly to lower citizenship inflows. These are not rounding errors in a small budget. They are close to the budget itself.

This is why the region's answer has hardened into a single position. In July, the heads of government of the participating Eastern Caribbean states issued a joint statement through Dominica's Office of the Prime Minister, declining to concede the date and asking instead for a framework to replace the financing a shutdown would remove. Browne has been the sharpest voice. The programs, he said, cannot simply be abandoned without viable, concrete, and credible replacement revenues, and his government will not be pressured into a unilateral phase-out (Antigua Observer). The message from the UN meeting was the same argument, delivered in person and one level higher.

Strip away the diplomacy and the problem is arithmetic. Brussels is asking five governments to give up a revenue line worth, in the largest case, close to a third of national output, and it is doing so without naming what comes in its place. The programs were built precisely because these islands carry narrow tax bases, high exposure to hurricanes, and limited access to cheap borrowing. Citizenship revenue filled that gap. Remove it on a fixed timetable and the hole does not close on its own. It becomes a financing question the region cannot answer alone, which is exactly the framework the prime ministers were asking Europe to help design.

There is a version of 2028 in which the programs do not end so much as change shape, with tighter vetting, higher price floors, shared regional standards, and closer coordination with Brussels buying the region continued access. There is another version in which the date arrives with no replacement framework and the five economies absorb the loss on their own. The distance between those two outcomes is the work of the next twenty months. The December report will show whether the interim conditions have moved Brussels at all, and whether continued dialogue, the phrase the prime ministers kept returning to, is a real channel or a courtesy.

This is the clearest test in the region of a question that reaches well beyond passports: whether small states can defend the revenue that keeps them solvent when a larger partner decides the model has to end. For now the region has done the only thing available to it before a deadline it did not choose. It has said no, together, and asked for a plan. What it does not yet have is the plan. The Ledger will follow this as one story with many chapters, and this is the next.

headline: Beckham's £39 million payday, and what the World Cup economy is really worth
stand: David Beckham's companies paid him a £39 million dividend, about US$51 million, on record profits driven by 2026 World Cup deals. The Caribbean sits next door to that money and rarely sees it.

blocks.x: David Beckham has taken a £39 million dividend from his business, roughly US$51 million, after his companies posted record profits of about £50 million on the back of commercial deals tied to the 2026 World Cup (IBTimes UK, Irish Examiner). It is the same money reported in different currencies, which is why some outlets ran $51 million and others €45 million.

For the Caribbean the number is a mirror. The 2026 World Cup is being played next door, across the United States, Canada and Mexico, in the same Concacaf region the region's own teams competed in this month. The commercial value that flows to a single ambassador dwarfs what most Caribbean federations earn from the sport in a decade.

The lesson the Ledger keeps returning to is that the money in global sport is made off the field, in licensing, image rights and endorsement, not on it. Beckham's dividend is a clean illustration of the gap between playing the game and owning a piece of it.

headline: India take the first ODI by eight wickets as Gill and Kohli answer Greaves
stand: West Indies made a competitive 295 and Justin Greaves reached a maiden hundred, but twin centuries from Shubman Gill and Virat Kohli chased it down with eight wickets to spare in Thiruvananthapuram.

blocks.x: West Indies gave themselves something to defend and still lost by a distance. Batting first in the opening one-day international at Thiruvananthapuram on September 27, they posted 295 for seven, built on Justin Greaves' maiden ODI century, 101 from 108 balls, with support from John Campbell and Amir Jangoo (ESPNcricinfo).

It was not enough. Shubman Gill made 110 and Virat Kohli an unbeaten 139 as India reached 300 for two with more than eight overs and eight wickets in hand. Kuldeep Yadav had earlier taken four for 40 to keep West Indies in check.

West Indies trail the three-match series one to nil, with the second game in Guwahati on September 30. For a side rebuilding toward the 2027 World Cup, the batting held up. The bowling, against two of the world's best chasers, did not.

headline: Montego Bay United go top as Jourdain Fletcher's goal settles it
stand: A first-half strike from Jourdain Fletcher and a third straight clean sheet beat Racing United one to nil and sent Montego Bay level at the top of the Jamaica Premier League.

blocks.x: Montego Bay United are level top of the Jamaica Premier League after a one to nil win over Racing United in Sunday's round, decided by a first-half goal from Jourdain Fletcher, the league's leading scorer. It was the club's third straight clean sheet.

The result put Montego Bay level with Tru-Juice on seven points, while Racing slipped to fourth. The defensive record is doing as much as Fletcher's goals: three shutouts in a row is title form this early in the season.

headline: Moody's lifts Trinidad and Tobago's outlook to stable at Ba2
stand: The agency moved the twin-island republic's outlook to stable, citing steadier energy revenue and fiscal repair, a modest vote of confidence before the 2027 budget.

blocks.x: Moody's has raised its outlook on Trinidad and Tobago to stable while affirming the rating at Ba2, pointing to steadier energy revenue and progress on the public finances. It is an upgrade in tone rather than rating, but a welcome one as the government frames its 2027 budget.

headline: Guyana's first-half crude exports reach US$15.05 billion
stand: Output near 902,000 barrels a day kept the Stabroek block scaling and Guyana the region's fastest-growing economy.

blocks.x: Guyana exported US$15.05 billion of crude in the first half of the year, with production running near 902,000 barrels a day as the Stabroek block continued to scale. The numbers keep Guyana the fastest-growing economy in the region by a wide margin, and the fiscal question is less about revenue than about how quickly it can be spent well.

headline: Anguilla's .ai windfall reaches US$232.2 million, one sixth of the economy
stand: Receipts from the artificial-intelligence internet suffix delivered a US$171 million surplus, turning a tiny territory's domain into its largest revenue line. Island in Focus.

blocks.x: Anguilla has found an unlikely fiscal engine in the alphabet. Receipts from .ai, the internet suffix the territory happens to own, reached US$232.2 million, about 16.5% of GDP, and delivered a US$171 million surplus. The artificial-intelligence boom that made every startup want a .ai address has quietly become the island's largest single revenue line.

headline: Jonquel Jones and the Liberty stun the top seed in the WNBA playoffs
stand: Bahamian forward Jonquel Jones led the eighth-seeded New York Liberty past the top-seeded Minnesota Lynx 91 to 75 in Game 1.

blocks.x: Jonquel Jones, from the Bahamas, helped the eighth-seeded New York Liberty upset the top-seeded Minnesota Lynx 91 to 75 in Game 1 of their WNBA playoff series. It is the kind of result that travels: a Caribbean athlete at the center of an American postseason upset.

headline: Cuba's Yordan Alvarez wins the American League batting title
stand: The Houston slugger finished at .316 as the Major League Baseball regular season closed, another Caribbean name atop an American leaderboard.

blocks.x: Yordan Alvarez, born in Cuba, won the American League batting title at .316 as the Major League Baseball regular season ended. The Caribbean's export of elite baseball talent is an old story, but the leaderboard at season's end is a reliable place to find it.

headline: TotalEnergies' GranMorgu is half-financed, with first oil targeted for mid-2028
stand: The Block 58 development moves Suriname toward its first offshore oil, with production planned for 2028.

blocks.x: TotalEnergies' GranMorgu project offshore Suriname is now about half financed, keeping first oil on track for the middle of 2028. It is the development that turns Suriname from an oil prospect into an oil producer, and its timeline is the one the whole economy is now planning around.

headline: Dominican Republic holds at 5.25% and opens new bank-capital rules
stand: The central bank kept its policy rate steady and moved to modernize capital requirements for the banking system.

blocks.x: The Dominican Republic's central bank held its policy rate at 5.25% and, in the same week, opened a revision of the capital rules that govern its banks. The rate hold was expected. The capital review is the more consequential move, aligning the region's largest economy closer to international standards.

headline: A Caribbean Sweep: Six Wins in One Night
stand: Jamaica, Suriname, St. Kitts and Nevis, Barbados, Guadeloupe and Cuba all won across the Concacaf Nations League on September 25, led by a stoppage-time winner in Kingston.

blocks.x: It was a night that belonged to the region. Across the Concacaf Nations League on September 25, six Caribbean sides walked off the field as winners, and one of them did it in the last breath of the match.

The signature moment came in Kingston. Jamaica beat Guatemala 3-2 at the National Stadium, with Renaldo Cephas settling it in the fourth minute of stoppage time. Palmer opened the scoring in the 37th minute and Burrell restored the lead in the 53rd, while Guatemala's Santis struck twice, in the second minute and the 67th. It was interim coach Rudolph Speid's first win in charge, and Cephas, with the decisive goal, was the man who made the night.

Suriname matched the drama on the road, winning 3-2 at Honduras in Group A. In League B the home sides held serve: St. Kitts and Nevis beat Bonaire 2-1, Barbados saw off Saint Lucia 2-0, and Guadeloupe and Cuba won as well. The one that got away was Martinique, beaten 3-1 at El Salvador. All results are per the Concacaf Nations League recap.

The wider story is momentum. Suriname, unbeaten on a difficult away trip, look like the side carrying the most belief, and St. Kitts and Nevis are quietly building. But the biggest question sits in Kingston, where a stoppage-time escape leaves fans asking whether the Reggae Boyz are ready to reclaim the region's top tier.
The weekend does not slow down. On Sunday, September 27, the West Indies women play their second one-day international in Harare, and the West Indies men open their one-day series in India.

headline: Guyana More Than Doubles Its 2026 Oil Revenue Forecast to US$6.5 Billion
stand: The Ministry of Finance mid-year report lifts Georgetown's projected petroleum take to US$6.4976 billion, a 136.8% jump from the US$2.8 billion first budgeted.
byline: The Caribbean Ledger, Business and Policy Desk

blocks.x: Guyana has more than doubled its forecast for 2026 oil revenue, with the Ministry of Finance mid-year report lifting the government's projected petroleum take to US$6.4976 billion. That is a 136.8% increase on the US$2.8 billion first written into the budget, and it resets the fiscal arithmetic for the fastest-growing economy in the hemisphere.

The revision rests on two forces the government names directly: firmer crude prices through the first half of the year, and faster cost recovery on the Stabroek block, which brings a larger share of production value to the treasury sooner. Together they move the needle by billions in a single half-year.

For a country that pumped its first barrel only at the end of 2019, the pace of the change is the story as much as the size. A doubling of the projected take is the kind of swing that decides how much a government can commit to infrastructure, transfers and its sovereign fund in the same year it earns it.

The figures are drawn from the Ministry of Finance mid-year report, carried through the Department of Public Information and Kaieteur News. The Ledger reports the government's stated take, not the gross export value of the crude.

headline: Royal Caribbean Buys Half of Jamaica's Sandals in a US$3 Billion Deal
stand: Royal Caribbean Group is taking a 50% stake in the Jamaica-founded Sandals and Beaches Resorts, tying the region's biggest cruise line to its best known all-inclusive brand.
byline: The Caribbean Ledger, Business and Policy Desk

blocks.x: Royal Caribbean Group is buying a 50% stake in Sandals and Beaches Resorts for about US$3 billion, in a deal announced on September 22 that binds the region's largest cruise operator to the Caribbean's best known all-inclusive brand.

The pairing is a bet on where Caribbean tourism spending is heading. A cruise line that moves millions of visitors through the region each year gains a land-based, high-margin resort footprint, while Sandals, built in Jamaica and run by the Stewart family, gains the balance sheet and distribution of a global operator.

For Jamaica, the transaction is a marker of the value now attached to a homegrown hospitality business. Sandals began with a single property in Montego Bay and became the flagship of Caribbean all-inclusive travel; a half-stake priced near US$3 billion sets a number on that four-decade build.
Terms are as announced by the companies on September 22, 2026. The Ledger will follow the regulatory and closing conditions as they are disclosed.

headline: Bank of Jamaica Holds at 5.50% Before Its September 28 Decision
stand: The policy rate stays at 5.50% as the Monetary Policy Committee weighs its next move, with a rate decision due September 28.

blocks.x: The Bank of Jamaica is holding its policy rate at 5.50% going into its September 28 decision, keeping the cost of money steady while the Monetary Policy Committee reads the inflation and currency data in front of it.

A hold is itself a signal. It tells banks and borrowers that the central bank sees no case yet to move in either direction, and it sets the backdrop for lending and deposit rates across the Jamaican system until the committee next speaks.

The September 28 meeting is the one to watch. Markets across the region take their cue from the largest independent-currency central bank in the English-speaking Caribbean, so the decision reaches well beyond Kingston.
The rate and the meeting date are from the Bank of Jamaica's published policy schedule.

headline: Barbados Reserves Near US$3 Billion as the Economy Grows 1.7%
stand: Foreign reserves sit close to US$3 billion, about 25.5 weeks of import cover, as first-quarter output rises 1.7%.

blocks.x: Barbados is holding foreign reserves close to US$3 billion, equal to about 25.5 weeks of import cover, according to the Central Bank of Barbados, while first-quarter output grew 1.7%.

For a pegged economy, reserves in weeks of import cover are the health check that matters most, and 25.5 weeks sits comfortably above the three-month line that signals strain. It is the number that keeps the Barbados dollar's peg to the US dollar credible.

The 1.7% growth read is modest but positive, and it comes on top of the reserve position rather than at its expense, a combination the island has worked deliberately toward since its 2018 restructuring.
Figures are from the Central Bank of Barbados quarterly review.

headline: Bahamas Outbound Travel Rose 7.1% in July
stand: Departures reached 180,831 in July, up 7.1%, a read on the pace of Bahamian travel and household spending.

blocks.x: Outbound travel from The Bahamas rose 7.1% in July, with departures reaching 180,831, according to the Central Bank of The Bahamas.

Outbound numbers are a demand signal. Rising departures point to households with the income and the confidence to travel, and they sit alongside the inbound tourism that carries the Bahamian economy as a read on the strength of the consumer.
The pace matters for a service economy where the tourism cycle drives employment, foreign exchange and the government's own revenue. A 7.1% monthly gain is a firm print.
The July figure is from the Central Bank of The Bahamas.

headline: Dominican Republic Sees Tourism Revenue Topping US$12.5 Billion in 2026
stand: The central bank projects tourism earnings above US$12.5 billion this year, keeping the sector the Dominican economy's largest foreign-exchange engine.

blocks.x: The Dominican Republic expects tourism revenue to top US$12.5 billion in 2026, according to a projection from the Banco Central de la República Dominicana, cementing the sector as the country's largest single source of foreign exchange.

The scale is the point. At more than US$12.5 billion, Dominican tourism earnings dwarf those of any single English-speaking Caribbean market, and they anchor a current account that funds imports and supports the peso.
The Dominican model, high-volume all-inclusive resorts feeding a steady stream of hard currency, is the one several smaller islands study when they debate how far to scale their own tourism plant.
The projection is from the Banco Central de la República Dominicana.

headline: Suriname's GranMorgu Stays on Course for First Oil in 2028
stand: TotalEnergies keeps the offshore GranMorgu development on track for first production in mid-2028, Suriname's entry into the producer club Guyana opened.
byline: The Caribbean Ledger, Business and Policy Desk

blocks.x: Suriname's GranMorgu project remains on track for first oil in mid-2028, TotalEnergies has indicated, keeping Paramaribo on schedule to follow its neighbor into offshore production.

GranMorgu is Suriname's entry into the club Guyana opened. The same deep-water geology that turned Georgetown into an oil economy runs across the maritime border, and first production in 2028 would begin to convert that geology into government revenue.

The lesson from Guyana is that the years between a final investment decision and first oil are the ones that decide whether a small state captures the windfall or spends it in advance. Suriname is now in that window.
The mid-2028 timeline is from TotalEnergies, reported through Pipeline and Gas Journal.

headline: Mottley Puts a Number on the Climate-Finance Gap at the UN
stand: Vulnerable states need about US$490 billion a year by 2030, against roughly US$90 billion flowing now, Barbados's prime minister told the United Nations.
byline: The Caribbean Ledger, Business and Policy Desk

blocks.x: Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley put hard numbers on the climate-finance gap at the United Nations, telling the assembly that vulnerable states need about US$490 billion a year by 2030 against roughly US$90 billion flowing to them now.

The gap is the argument. A more than fivefold shortfall between what small and climate-exposed states need and what they receive is the case Mottley has carried from Bridgetown to every major forum, and the frame behind the Bridgetown Initiative on reforming development finance.

For the Caribbean the stakes are concrete. The same islands that contribute least to emissions carry the highest catastrophe exposure, and the finance to adapt is the difference between recovering from a storm and being set back a decade by one.
The figures are from Prime Minister Mottley's remarks at the United Nations on September 24, 2026.

headline: Haiti Stun Trinidad and Tobago 3-2 With Two Stoppage-Time Goals
stand: Haiti scored twice deep in stoppage time to beat Trinidad and Tobago in the Concacaf Nations League.

blocks.x: Haiti beat Trinidad and Tobago 3-2 in the Concacaf Nations League, scoring twice deep in stoppage time to turn a draw into a win in the final seconds.

It was a result decided after the ninetieth minute, the kind that swings a group. Trinidad and Tobago will rue two goals conceded when the match looked saved; Haiti take the full three points and the momentum.

For two Caribbean football nations the Nations League is the stage where regional bragging rights and World Cup pathways are contested, and a stoppage-time turnaround is the sort of night that is remembered.
Match result and timing are per Concacaf.

headline: Guyana and Trinidad Sign a US-Led Hemispheric Pact at the United Nations
stand: Two CARICOM states have put their names to a fifteen-nation statement that binds security to economics, including investment screening and critical-minerals supply chains.
byline: The Caribbean Ledger, Business and Policy Desk

blocks.x: Guyana and Trinidad and Tobago have signed a United States-convened statement on hemispheric cooperation at the United Nations, joining a fifteen-nation group in what Washington titled the Joint Statement on Defending Hemispheric Sovereignty. For two CARICOM members, it is a notable alignment with the United States at a moment of tension in regional waters.

The signatories are the United States alongside Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guyana, Honduras, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, and Trinidad and Tobago. The statement sets three pillars: economic, security, and multilateral.
The economic pillar is the part to watch

For a business paper the economic commitments matter most. Members agree to deeper trade cooperation, to investment-screening mechanisms, and to safeguarding critical-minerals supply chains, alongside coordinated sanctions against designated narco-terrorist organizations. Guyana said the following day that it will move to sanction named groups. Investment screening in particular carries real consequences for small, capital-hungry states that court foreign money, and it is worth watching how Georgetown and Port of Spain apply it.

The timing is its own story. The signing came the same week Port of Spain reopened relations with Caracas, leaving Trinidad and Tobago straddling Washington and Venezuela in a single news cycle. Sovereignty, standing, and economic exposure for small states all sit inside one document.

Sources: U.S. State Department, Joint Statement on Defending Hemispheric Sovereignty (September 22, 2026); with corroboration from Al Jazeera, Demerara Waves and News Room Guyana. Details are as reported by those outlets.

headline: Trinidad and Venezuela Declare a New Era, With Energy in the Frame
stand: Prime Minister Persad-Bissessar and Venezuela's Delcy Rodriguez signed a cooperation statement in New York, reviving the question of cross-border gas.
byline: The Caribbean Ledger, Business and Policy Desk

blocks.x: Trinidad and Tobago and Venezuela have declared what both sides called a new era in their relationship. Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar and Venezuelan Vice President Delcy Rodriguez signed a joint statement in New York committing to cooperation on trade, energy, security, and air connectivity, with reciprocal visits planned.

The statement is a framework, and no gas volumes or figures were disclosed. But the energy line is the one that matters for Port of Spain. Trinidad's gas output has been in long decline, and cross-border fields shared with Venezuela have for years been the most obvious source of new supply. A thaw, even a cautious one, revives a prospect that sanctions and politics had frozen.

The straddle is hard to miss. In the same week, Trinidad and Tobago put its name to a United States-led hemispheric statement, then warmed relations with Caracas. For a small energy economy caught between two larger powers, both moves are about the same thing: keeping the gas flowing.
Sources: CNC3, Trinidad Express, TTT News and the Jamaica Observer (September 23, 2026). The joint-statement text was not yet public at the time of writing.

headline: Jamaica Counts the Cost of Melissa as the Recovery Bill Comes Due
stand: The prime minister put hurricane damage near 55% of GDP as the June-quarter contraction eased, days before the Bank of Jamaica's next rate decision.

blocks.x: Jamaica is beginning to put numbers to the cost of Hurricane Melissa. At a ceremony marking a US$5 million European Union grant for national reconstruction, routed through the World Bank, Prime Minister Andrew Holness put the storm's damage at roughly 55% of gross domestic product, a figure that captures how heavily the hurricane fell on the island's economy.

items.l: Melissa damage as a share of GDP (PM)
June-quarter contraction, easing from 7.1%
Next Bank of Jamaica rate decision

blocks.x: Cabinet reported the June-quarter contraction easing to 2.9%, from 7.1% and then 4.1% in prior quarters, a sign the worst of the shock has passed even as the rebuilding bill mounts. The opposition finance spokesman, Julian Robinson, put new borrowing at J$30 billion against a revenue shortfall of J$28.7 billion; those are opposition figures and await official confirmation.

The fiscal reckoning lands three business days before the Bank of Jamaica's next rate decision on September 28. The central bank has held its policy rate at 5.50%, with August inflation at 7.9%, still above target. A recovery that needs cheap money and a central bank fighting prices are not easily reconciled, and Melissa has sharpened the tension.
Sources: the Jamaica Gleaner (September 23, 2026); Bank of Jamaica; and STATIN. Opposition borrowing figures are attributed and unconfirmed.

headline: Bermuda's Company Count Falls to a Four-Year Low as the New Tax Bites
stand: Local company registrations dropped 10.1% year on year, the first hard read on how the island's 15% corporate tax is reshaping its international-business base.

blocks.x: The number of local companies registered in Bermuda fell to 3,660 at the end of the first quarter, down 442, or 10.1%, on the year, and the fewest since the third quarter of 2021. Total registrations dropped to 15,122, down 1,168 or 7.2%, with exempted companies at 9,702.

items.l: Local companies, a four-year low
Year-on-year fall
Corporate income tax, from 2025

blocks.x: The government links the decline to Bermuda's 15% corporate income tax, introduced in 2025 for groups with global revenue above 750 million euros, part of the OECD-led global minimum-tax regime. This is the first hard data on how that tax is reshaping one of the region's premier offshore centers, and it is a template read for every other Caribbean jurisdiction that has built an economy on international business.

The question the numbers raise is whether this is a one-time adjustment as groups restructure, or the start of a longer erosion of the registration base that has underwritten Bermuda's public finances for decades.
Source: The Royal Gazette (September 23, 2026), citing the Quarterly Bulletin of Statistics and Minister Jason Hayward.

headline: The US Virgin Islands Calls Its Finances Precarious as Tax Take Falls
stand: Individual income-tax collections fell US$31.7 million as a US$1.64 billion budget advances and a credit line is already heavily drawn.

blocks.x: The US Virgin Islands has described its finances as precarious as income-tax revenue slides. Individual income-tax collections fell to US$403 million in the 2026 fiscal year, from US$434.7 million, a drop of US$31.7 million, according to the territory's Legislature Budget Committee.

items.l: Fall in individual income-tax take
Proposed FY2027 budget
Drawn of a US$150M credit line

blocks.x: A proposed US$1.64 billion budget for fiscal 2027 is advancing even as the territory has already drawn US$124.78 million of a US$150 million credit line. It is a northern-territory fiscal-stress signal set against slow recovery spending, and it stands in contrast to the record visitor numbers the islands have reported this year.
Source: VI Consortium (September 22, 2026), citing the Virgin Islands Legislature Budget Committee.

headline: A Cayman Bill Would Force the Power Company to Retender Its Fuel
stand: Proposed legislation would let the regulator require Caribbean Utilities Company to competitively retender a fuel supply now split between two firms.

blocks.x: A bill before the Cayman Islands would let the utility regulator require the Caribbean Utilities Company to competitively retender its fuel supply, currently split about 60% to Rubis and 40% to Sol on roughly 40 million imperial gallons a year.

The Fuel Market Regulation Amendment Bill, brought by member of parliament Chris Saunders, goes to the heart of electricity pricing in one of the region's higher-cost power markets. Fuel is the single largest input into an island utility's bills, and who supplies it, and at what price, flows straight through to every household and business.

The read-across is regional. Many Caribbean islands run a single utility buying fuel from one or two suppliers on long-standing terms, and a move to force competitive tendering in Cayman will be watched by consumer advocates and regulators across the basin.
Source: the Cayman Compass (September 22, 2026), with a response from the regulator OfReg.

headline: Curacao's Gaming Regulator Confirms a Months-Long Portal Breach
stand: The Curacao Gaming Authority says its online licensing portal was accessed without authorization for close to ten months, a credibility test for a pillar industry.

blocks.x: The Curacao Gaming Authority has confirmed that its online licensing portal was accessed without authorization for roughly ten months, from about December 2025 to September 2026. The regulator disclosed the breach this week.

Online gaming is a pillar of Curacao's economy and the centerpiece of its new licensing regime under the National Ordinance on Games of Chance, which the island has promoted as a more credible, better-regulated framework than its old model. A breach at the regulator itself is therefore a credibility question for the whole sector, not only an IT incident.

The Ledger is not printing any figure for the volume of data involved, because the authority has not confirmed one. What is confirmed is the fact of the intrusion and its duration, and that alone is material for an industry that sells trust to operators worldwide.
Source: Curacao Gaming Authority statement (September 22, 2026), via the Curacao Chronicle. Unverified data-extraction claims are held.

headline: Baha Mar Plans a New US$700 Million Bahamas Hotel
stand: The resort operator says it will break ground on a new beachfront hotel within months, once final permits clear.

blocks.x: Baha Mar, the mega-resort operator in Nassau, says it will break ground on a new US$700 million beachfront hotel within months, once final permits are cleared. It would be a fresh expansion of one of the largest tourism developments in the Caribbean.

For The Bahamas, a US$700 million commitment is a vote of confidence in the country's tourism engine at a time when several neighbors are working to defend their own arrival numbers. Foreign direct investment of this scale is both a jobs story and a signal to other developers weighing the region.

The Ledger notes the project is announced rather than under way, and will confirm the permit status and the groundbreaking when they are set. The number and the intent are on the record; the shovel is not yet in the ground.
Source: The Nassau Guardian, Business (September 22, 2026).

headline: Guyana's Oil Exports Hit a Record US$15 Billion in the First Half
stand: Output above 900,000 barrels a day pushed first-half export earnings to a record, with the government's own take approaching US$2 billion.

blocks.x: Guyana's oil exports reached a record US$15 billion in the first half of 2026, as production offshore the Stabroek Block climbed above 900,000 barrels a day. The government's own share of that trade approached US$2 billion, according to the Department of Public Information.

items.l: First-half oil exports, a record
Government take in the half
Barrels a day of production

blocks.x: The figure sits alongside the Ministry of Finance mid-year report, which lifted the full-year petroleum forecast sharply on higher prices and faster cost recovery. Together they describe an economy whose scale is now set less by its own decisions than by the pace at which the Stabroek partners can bring barrels to market.

For the wider Caribbean the question is no longer whether Guyana is rich, but whether the windfall becomes regional capital or stays a national one. Every extra billion in government revenue is a billion that could anchor a regional development bank, a shared fund, or simply more Guyanese demand for Caribbean goods and labor. The export record is the clearest sign yet of how much is now in play.
Source: Guyana Department of Public Information (September 16, 2026). Figures are as reported by that office.

headline: Cuba Faces the Region's Steepest Contraction, ECLAC Projects a 10.3% Fall
stand: The UN's regional commission expects the Cuban economy to shrink 10.3% in 2026, the deepest decline anywhere in Latin America and the Caribbean.

blocks.x: The Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean projects that Cuba's economy will contract 10.3% in 2026, the steepest fall of any country in the region. It is a figure that marks Cuba as an outlier at the bottom of the Caribbean's growth table in a year when most of the basin is expanding.

items.l: Projected 2026 contraction
Steepest decline in Latin America and the Caribbean

blocks.x: For a paper that reads the whole basin as one, Cuba's trajectory matters beyond its borders. It shapes migration pressure across the northern Caribbean, the flow of remittances, and the calculations of every government weighing its own exposure to fuel, food and foreign exchange. A contraction of this depth in one of the region's largest populations is a regional variable, not a national footnote.
Source: Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, ECLAC (September 10, 2026). The projection is as published by ECLAC.

headline: St. Vincent Loses Its Only US Nonstop as Delta Ends the Atlanta Route
stand: Delta Air Lines permanently ended its Atlanta to Argyle service on September 5, cutting the country's single nonstop link to the United States.

blocks.x: St. Vincent and the Grenadines has lost its only nonstop air link to the United States. Delta Air Lines permanently ended its Atlanta to Argyle International service on September 5, removing the single route that connected the country directly to a US hub.

For a small tourism economy, a nonstop to a major American hub is not a convenience, it is infrastructure. Its loss lengthens every visitor's journey, raises the effective cost of a holiday, and hands an advantage to neighboring islands that still hold their direct US service. Argyle International was built precisely to win this kind of connectivity, which makes the withdrawal a setback to the case the airport was meant to prove.

The question now is whether another carrier fills the gap or whether the route was cut because the traffic was not there. Either answer shapes how St. Vincent sells itself for the coming winter season, the stretch when North American arrivals matter most.
Source: Delta Air Lines schedule change (effective September 5, 2026), as reported in the Ledger's basin sweep.

headline: Sint Maarten and Curacao Turn On Deposit Insurance from September 28
stand: A new Deposit Guarantee Scheme protects bank deposits up to Cg 50,000 and credit-union deposits up to Cg 25,000 per depositor across the monetary union.

blocks.x: From September 28, savers in Sint Maarten and Curacao gain formal protection for their money for the first time under a Deposit Guarantee Scheme from the Central Bank of Curacao and Sint Maarten. Bank deposits are covered up to Cg 50,000 per depositor, and credit-union deposits up to Cg 25,000.

items.l: Bank deposit cover, per depositor
Credit-union cover, per depositor
Scheme takes effect

blocks.x: Deposit insurance is one of the quiet foundations of a modern financial system. It turns a bank run from a rational panic into an unnecessary one, because a covered saver has no reason to rush the door. For a monetary union that has worked through the difficult resolution of failed institutions, putting a guarantee behind the ordinary depositor is a signal of stability as much as a piece of consumer protection.

The measure also draws a clear line under who is protected and to what limit, which is itself useful information for households deciding where and how to hold their savings. The caps are per depositor, so the practical planning point for a saver above the limit is how deposits are spread.
Source: Central Bank of Curacao and Sint Maarten (CBCS) and the Ministry of Finance, scheme effective September 28, 2026.

headline: St. Kitts and Nevis Opens Its First Retail Bond to the Ordinary Saver
stand: The government's inaugural EC$5 million retail bond pays 4.5% and lets residents across the currency union lend from as little as EC$500.

blocks.x: St. Kitts and Nevis has opened its first retail bond, putting government debt within reach of ordinary savers for the first time. The inaugural offer, announced by the Saint Kitts and Nevis Information Service on September 22, pays 4.5% a year over two years and can be bought from as little as EC$500, a deliberate move to turn savers into investors across the Eastern Caribbean Currency Union.

items.l: Annual coupon, paid twice a year
Minimum investment, in EC$100 steps
Total the government is raising
Tenor, principal repaid at maturity

blocks.x: The terms

The issue raises EC$5.0 million. An individual may invest from EC$500 up to EC$125,000, a cap set at 2.5% of the issue so no single buyer dominates it. The bond runs two years and repays principal in full at maturity, with interest paid semiannually. The subscription window is open from September 22 through October 23, 2026, and the bonds are bought through approved brokers on the Regional Government Securities Market, namely the St. Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla National Bank and the Bank of Nevis. Individuals, residents and non-governmental organizations across the currency union are eligible, according to WINN FM.
Why it matters

The point is inclusion. “This bond is not simply a financial product,” Financial Secretary Carlton Pogson said. “It reflects a commitment to prudent management, confidence in the future, and a belief in the strength of our people.” The Governor of the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, Timothy Antoine, framed it as a habit the region needs to build, calling it “a steady, low-risk opportunity for you to get in the game, understand these things, and build good habits.”

For the wider Caribbean the significance is the template. A small state opening its debt to its own citizens, in amounts a working household can manage, deepens the regional securities market and offers a model other Eastern Caribbean governments can copy. If it draws real retail demand, the ordinary saver becomes a lender to the state, and the state gains a funding base that does not depend on foreign banks.
Sources: the Saint Kitts and Nevis Information Service (September 22, 2026); WINN FM; ABS TV Antigua and Barbuda; and the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank. Terms are as reported by those outlets.

headline: The On-Ramp: Why a Caribbean Paper Watches American College Sport
stand: Before the NBA, MLB or the NFL, the Caribbean athlete usually passes through an American campus. The scholarship is the real story.

blocks.x: For most Caribbean athletes who reach the top American leagues, the first stop is not a professional club. It is a college campus, on a scholarship that is as much an education story as a sports one. That is why the Ledger treats college basketball, baseball and track as the on-ramp rather than as a distant curiosity.

items.l: The gatekeeper: eligibility and scholarships run through the NCAA Eligibility Center
Feeder sports we track: basketball, baseball, and track and field
Typical campus time before a pro draft for a top recruit

blocks.x: The scholarship is the story

American athletic scholarships are, for a Caribbean family, one of the few routes to a funded United States degree, and the NCAA sets the terms through its Eligibility Center. For every island recruit who reaches a professional league, many more use the scholarship to earn a degree and return home, which makes the college game a development story as much as a sporting one.
Where the leagues begin

College basketball is the direct feeder to the NBA, college baseball to Major League Baseball through the draft, and college track has long carried the region's sprinters onto the world stage. The Caribbean recruit who signs with a Division I program in the autumn is the professional prospect of two or three years on. Follow the signing, and you are watching the pipeline fill in real time.

The honest note for this desk: at this stage we cover the college game through the recruits and the scholarships, the parts with a clear Caribbean stake, and add fuller results as the sports data layer comes online.

Sources: the NCAA Eligibility Center and NCAA scholarship guidance on athletic scholarships and eligibility. Figures on typical timelines are general and will be attributed to specific recruits as we cover them.

headline: From the Island to the End Zone: The Caribbean's Quiet NFL Lineage
stand: American football has no Caribbean league, yet the region has fed the NFL for decades, most visibly through its Haitian and Jamaican-born players.

blocks.x: American football is the one major league with no Caribbean competition feeding it, no island academies, no regional draft. And yet the NFL has drawn on the Caribbean for decades, mostly through the diaspora born in the region or raised by parents who left it.

items.l: Countries with their own NFL birthplace registries at Pro-Football-Reference: Jamaica and Haiti
The main channel: island families settled in the United States and Canada
Caribbean-based feeder leagues, unlike baseball and cricket

blocks.x: A lineage you can count

Pro-Football-Reference, the sport's standard record, keeps birthplace lists that include players born in Jamaica and in Haiti, a small but real roll that stretches back across eras. The Haitian Times has profiled the coaches and players representing the Haitian diaspora in the league, and Caribbean Beat has traced the arc from island to end zone. The pattern is consistent: the talent is Caribbean by blood and family, American by the field it plays on.
Why the Ledger covers it

For a Caribbean business paper the NFL is not a home league, it is a diaspora story and a money story. A player of Haitian or Jamaican heritage who reaches the league becomes a figure the region claims, a philanthropist who often turns back toward home, and a marker of the diaspora's reach. That is the lens we cover it through, the same way we read the Premier League and Major League Baseball.

The honest note for this desk: with no Caribbean feeder league, our NFL coverage will be selective by design, following the players and coaches with genuine island ties rather than every result. Live weekly scores are part of the data layer that arrives with the sports feed, once the paper can fund it.

Sources: Pro-Football-Reference birthplace registries (Jamaica, Haiti); The Haitian Times (“NFL coaches and players representing the Haitian Diaspora”); Caribbean Beat (“From island to end zone”). Player and roster details are as recorded by those outlets.

headline: Before the Tip-Off: The Caribbean Bloodlines in the NBA
stand: With the season weeks away, the league's Caribbean thread runs through the Dominican Republic's national-team stars and a widening group of island-born players.

blocks.x: The NBA season is still weeks from tip-off, which makes the quiet weeks of the calendar the right time to map the Caribbean's place in it. It is smaller than the region's footprint in baseball, but it is growing, and it runs most clearly through the Dominican Republic.

items.l: Dominican Republic, the region's strongest NBA national-team presence
NBA pre-season opens in October, the regular season late in the month
The winter feeder: NCAA basketball, where island recruits arrive first

blocks.x: The Dominican thread

The Dominican Republic has put the region's most recognizable names on NBA floors and behind its own national team, with veteran big man Al Horford, born in the Dominican Republic, the longest-standing example, and Karl-Anthony Towns, who has represented the Dominican Republic internationally, the most prominent of the current generation. Their national-team service is what ties the league back to the islands, turning an American competition into something Caribbean fans follow as partly their own.
The college on-ramp

The path into the league still runs through American college basketball, which is why the Ledger will cover the NCAA game as the Caribbean's on-ramp rather than as a foreign curiosity. The island recruit who signs with a Division I program in the autumn is the NBA prospect of two or three years on, and that is the story to follow through the winter.

The honest note for this desk: at this point in the calendar there are no games to report, only rosters and preparation. We will carry results once the pre-season opens in October, and until then we cover the league as what it is for the region right now, a pipeline and a point of pride.
Sources: NBA and FIBA national-team records for the Dominican Republic (Horford, Towns); league calendar per the NBA. Rosters are as recorded ahead of the 2026-27 season.

headline: The Islands Built This Game: The Caribbean's Mark on the 2026 Major League Season
stand: As the pennant races close, the season's standout hitting has again carried Dominican, Venezuelan and Cuban names, the pattern of a game the Caribbean helped make.

blocks.x: No region shapes Major League Baseball the way the Caribbean does. Year after year the Dominican Republic sends more players to the majors than any country outside the United States, and 2026 has again been a season written in Caribbean names as the pennant races close.

items.l: Game hitting streak to open 2026 by Ildemaro Vargas, a Venezuelan-born record
Yandy Díaz's league-leading average at midseason (Cuban-born)
Dominican Republic, the top source of foreign-born MLB players

blocks.x: A season in Caribbean names

The Arizona Diamondbacks' Ildemaro Vargas, born in Venezuela, opened the 2026 season with a 24-game hitting streak, the longest ever by a Venezuelan-born player, according to the record of the 2026 season. Cuba's Yandy Díaz led the American League in batting average at midseason at .336. Dominican infielder Otto López was among the National League's hits leaders for the Miami Marlins. None of this is new in kind. It is the annual proof of a pipeline the region has run for half a century.
The winter game feeds the summer one

That pipeline does not begin in spring training. It begins in the region's own winter leagues and the Caribbean Series, the February championship that draws the professional champions of the Dominican Republic, Venezuela, Puerto Rico, Mexico and their neighbors, and that has long served as both a showcase and a scouting ground for the majors.

For the Ledger, the economic reading is plain. The academies that clubs run across the Dominican Republic are among the largest private investments in Caribbean youth sport, and the signing bonuses and salaries that follow are a genuine export line for the region. The talent leaves, but the money, the training and the prestige come home.

Sources: the 2026 Major League Baseball season record (Vargas, Díaz, López, division standings); Major League Baseball on country-of-origin data. Season figures are as reported to date and will be updated as the postseason is set.

headline: The Caribbean's Game Abroad: Jamaica's Stars Anchor a New Season in England and America
stand: As the Premier League settles into 2026-27 and Major League Soccer runs to its playoffs, the Caribbean's biggest export remains its footballers.

blocks.x: The Caribbean rarely sends a club to the top of the English or American game, but it sends the players who decide matches there. As the Premier League settles into its 2026-27 season and Major League Soccer turns toward its autumn playoffs, the region's footprint is easiest to read through Jamaica, whose leading players have built their careers in exactly these two leagues.

items.l: Leagues where Jamaica's core plays: England and the United States
A World Cup year, the sport's largest audience
Reggae Boyz goalkeeper anchoring an MLS side, Andre Blake at Philadelphia

blocks.x: The Premier League contingent

Winger Leon Bailey and forward Michail Antonio are the names that carry Jamaica's profile in England, a lineage of Reggae Boyz who reached the Premier League and then pulled the national team up with them, as Goal has documented in tracing Jamaica's rise. Their value to the islands is not only the goals. It is the visibility, the pathway they mark for the next player in Kingston or Montego Bay who now believes the route runs all the way to the top division in England.
The American anchor

In Major League Soccer, Jamaica's presence is most visible in goal. Andre Blake has been the mainstay at the Philadelphia Union for a decade, one of the most decorated goalkeepers in the league's history, and the club has openly tied its fortunes and Jamaica's to his form. As MLS runs to its playoffs, he is the clearest example of a Caribbean player who did not pass through Europe to reach the elite, but built an elite career in the American game itself.

That matters for the Ledger's readers because it is also an economic story. A Caribbean footballer in the Premier League or MLS is a remittance engine, a brand, and a recruiter for the academies back home, and 2026, a World Cup year and the sport's largest stage, is when that value peaks. The region does not yet own a club at that level. It owns something the clubs cannot do without.

Sources: Goal (“Michail Antonio, Leon Bailey and Jamaica's Premier League stars”); Philadelphia Union club records on Andre Blake; the Jamaica Observer's 2026 coverage of the Reggae Boyz. Figures and squad details are as reported by those outlets.

headline: Guyana Nearly Doubles Its 2026 Oil-Revenue Forecast to About US$6.5 Billion
stand: The Ministry of Finance 2026 Mid-Year Report raised projected full-year petroleum revenue roughly 137%, to about US$6.5 billion, on first-half crude exports of US$15.05 billion and output near 902,000 barrels per day.

blocks.x: Guyana's Ministry of Finance said real GDP expanded 33.3% in the first half of 2026 and raised its full-year growth forecast to 20.8%, according to the 2026 Mid-Year Report published September 15. Crude oil exports topped US$15.05 billion over the six months, and Georgetown more than doubled its 2026 petroleum revenue projection to about US$6.5 billion, made up of US$5.9 billion in profit oil and US$508.1 million in royalties.

items.l: 2026 oil-revenue forecast, up from US$2.8B
First-half crude exports
First-half real GDP growth
Oil lifts now expected in 2026, up from 40

blocks.x: A revision that resets the basin

The revision, about 137% above the earlier US$2.8 billion projection, reflects faster repayment of ExxonMobil's Stabroek Block costs and firmer world prices, the ministry said. Georgetown now expects 84 oil lifts this year rather than 40, with output near 902,000 barrels per day.

A near-doubling of a sovereign's oil take resets the region's fastest-growing economy and sharpens every downstream question the basin now faces, from oil-fund withdrawal rules and capacity spending to the Guyana and Suriname producer race, as neighboring states press their own case for development financing and debt relief.
Source: Guyana Ministry of Finance, Mid-Year Report 2026, via the Department of Public Information (September 15, 2026) and Kaieteur News (September 19, 2026).

headline: Anguilla Posts a Record First Half of 81,907 Stayover Visitors
stand: First-half stayover arrivals rose 19.9% from a year earlier, an added 13,620 visitors and the island's strongest opening half on record.

blocks.x: Anguilla recorded 81,907 stayover visitors in the first half of 2026, up 19.9% from 68,287 a year earlier, according to the island's Statistics Department. The gain of 13,620 visitors is the territory's strongest opening half on record.
A small territory running high-yield tourism beside its .ai domain income shows how the least-watched economies are compounding fastest when a single niche lands.
Source: Anguilla Statistics Department, via Caribbean National Weekly (September 16, 2026).

headline: Cayman Registered Funds Cross 31,000
stand: Cayman-registered funds reached 31,145 at the half-year mark, a net gain of 547 in six months, per the Cayman Islands Monetary Authority's second-quarter 2026 statistics.

blocks.x: The number of funds registered in the Cayman Islands reached 31,145 at the half-year mark, made up of 18,132 private funds and 13,013 mutual funds, a net gain of 547 over six months, according to Cayman Islands Monetary Authority statistics for the second quarter of 2026.
The region's largest financial-services center is still adding mandates, a steady earner that anchors public revenue in a way tourism cannot.
Source: CIMA, via Cayman Finance (July 14, 2026).

headline: Bermuda Moves Toward a New Parametric Insurer Class
stand: The Bermuda Monetary Authority is targeting a fourth-quarter 2026 rollout of a Parametric Special Purpose Insurer class, and says it will judge contracts by the substance of the risk transfer, not their form.

blocks.x: The Bermuda Monetary Authority is targeting a fourth-quarter 2026 rollout of a Parametric Special Purpose Insurer class, and on September 17 confirmed it will judge contracts by the substance of the risk transfer rather than their contractual form.
Parametric cover pays out on a measured trigger such as wind speed. A Bermuda-regulated class for it speaks straight to how a hurricane-exposed region prices disaster risk.
Source: Artemis.bm (September 17, 2026).

headline: Dominican Republic Growth Holds at 4.5% Through July
stand: Banco Central data show 4.5% expansion in the first seven months of 2026, with August inflation at 5.13% and reserves near US$15.43 billion.

blocks.x: The Dominican Republic economy grew 4.5% in January through July 2026, according to Banco Central data, with August inflation at 5.13% and net international reserves near US$15.43 billion. The central bank held its policy rate at 5.25% on August 31.
The basin's largest economy is running near trend with contained inflation, a useful benchmark for neighbors managing tighter fiscal room.
Source: Banco Central de la República Dominicana (September 21, 2026).

headline: Afreximbank Lifts Its CARICOM Financing Cap to US$5 Billion
stand: Caribbean governments used the fifth Africa-CARICOM Day to press a shared trade, finance and reparatory-justice agenda, with Afreximbank's regional financing ceiling now at a record US$5 billion.

blocks.x: Afreximbank has raised its CARICOM financing ceiling to a record US$5 billion, and Caribbean governments used the fifth Africa-CARICOM Day on September 7 to press a shared trade, finance and reparatory-justice agenda.
It is the region's most direct South-South money-and-standing story, small states leaning on African institutions to diversify away from traditional Western lenders.
Source: Afreximbank.

headline: Haiti Inflation Slows to 18.9%
stand: The Bank of the Republic of Haiti reported annual inflation easing to 18.9% in June 2026 from 32.2% last October, with a stable exchange rate for more than two years and about US$1.9 billion in reserves.

blocks.x: The Bank of the Republic of Haiti, marking its 47th anniversary, reported annual inflation easing to 18.9% in June 2026, down from 32.2% in October 2025. The bank cited a stable exchange rate for more than two years and about US$1.9 billion in reserves, roughly eight months of imports.
Monetary stabilization amid a security and governance crisis is a rare positive marker, and the reserve cushion buys the authorities time.
Source: Banque de la République d'Haïti (September 7, 2026).

headline: The BES Islands, Where One Currency Meets Three Price Stories
stand: Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba share the US dollar and De Nederlandsche Bank, yet second-quarter data show three distinct inflation paths, led by transport costs.

blocks.x: Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba share the US dollar, De Nederlandsche Bank as monetary authority, and a common tie to the Netherlands, yet the latest official price data show three distinct inflation paths. Statistics Netherlands put second-quarter 2026 year-over-year inflation at 3.3% on Bonaire, 5.0% on Saba and 5.2% on Sint Eustatius, with transport the common driver, petrol up 20.9% and flights up about 9% on Saba.

The read for the wider basin is about scale and exposure. The two smallest islands carry the higher inflation because a handful of imported cost lines, above all fuel and air links, move their whole index. When the basket is small and almost entirely imported, a single freight or fuel move lands as headline inflation rather than a line item. The dollarized BES islands cannot lean on a domestic monetary lever to soften it, which puts the weight on fiscal transfers and supply logistics.
Source: Statistics Netherlands (CBS), via BES-Reporter (July 23, 2026).
