A canal that runs short can send volume to hubs that can hold it, and the islands that have invested in deepwater capacity may capture some of the traffic the locks turn away.
The weather now sets the price of a container, and the Caribbean imports the weather's decisions.
The longer signal

The deeper lesson is about climate as a line item. A drought a thousand miles away is now a factor in a Caribbean household budget, because the region's supply chains run through a waterway that depends on rain. Resilience used to mean sea walls and reserves. It increasingly means watching the reservoirs that feed the routes our goods travel, and building the ports and the buffers that let us bend when a distant lake runs low. The Ledger will track the canal's slot count the way it tracks a policy rate, because for an importing region, that number is a price.

sources: Reuters (Elida Moreno); Panama Canal Authority; Newsroom Panama; Euronews

headline: The Flights Home, and the Bill Haiti Cannot Pay
stand: With Temporary Protected Status ended, deportation flights to Haiti have resumed. The question the numbers force is whether the country, and the remittances that keep it standing, can absorb the return.

blocks.title: 160+ Haitians Deported As ICE Cracks Down After TPS Termination

blocks.x: The first ICE deportation flight to Haiti since the end of Temporary Protected Status landed in Cap-Haitien this week, part of a crackdown that follows the formal termination of the status that had shielded roughly 300,000 Haitians in the United States. A court confirmed the protections are no longer in place, and reporting put more than 160 people on the recent removals.
What TPS was holding up

The status did two things at once. It kept people from being sent back to a country the United States itself had warned Americans not to visit, and it let them work legally, which meant it let them send money home. That second function is the one with a number attached, because remittances are not charity in Haiti. They are the economy.

Money sent home by Haitians abroad runs to a fifth or more of the country's output, one of the highest ratios in the world. Much of it comes from the United States, and much of that from people whose ability to earn depended on the very status that has now lapsed. Take away the work permit and you do not only change one family's fortunes. You thin the single largest inflow the Haitian economy has.
A return into a crisis

The people stepping off these flights are returning to a country still gripped by gang violence and governed by a fragile transitional authority, the same conditions the Ledger has covered as Haiti prepares for its first elections in a decade. A wave of returnees arriving with no work, into a place with little to offer them, is a humanitarian strain and an economic one at the same time.
Remittances are not charity in Haiti. They are the economy.
Why the whole region is watching

This is not only a Haitian story. Across the Caribbean, hundreds of thousands of people live in the United States on statuses that can be reviewed, and the diaspora that sends money to Jamaica, to the Dominican Republic and to the Eastern Caribbean is reading Haiti's experience as a warning about how quickly the ground can shift. The remittance flows that several Caribbean economies count on more than any export are, in the end, a policy decision made in Washington. The Ledger will follow the flights, and the money, because in this region the two move together.

sources: New York Post; The Washington Post; NBC News; CNN; USCIS

headline: A Tremor Erased in Minutes, and the Distance to the Caribbean
stand: American regulators have cleared a focused-ultrasound treatment that can quiet a Parkinson's tremor without a single incision. The advance is real. The question for the region is who gets to reach it.

blocks.title: A neuroradiologist on the newly approved Parkinson's therapy that can erase tremor

blocks.x: A treatment that uses focused ultrasound to still the tremor of Parkinson's disease, without cutting into the skull, has been approved for use on both sides of the body, and the images that carried the story showed a patient's yearslong shaking stop within minutes. It is one of a run of non-invasive advances that are changing what a diagnosis of a movement disorder means.
What the treatment does

The procedure guides beams of ultrasound to a precise point deep in the brain, using an MRI scanner to aim, and quiets the circuit that drives the tremor. There is no incision and no implant. For patients who cannot tolerate surgery or the medication route, it offers relief that used to require an operation, and it does it in a single session.
Why the Ledger runs a medical story

Global Lens is about how the wider world reaches the Caribbean, and medicine is one of the clearest cases. An advance approved in the United States does not arrive here on its own. It arrives through the machines a hospital can afford, the specialists it can keep, and the price a family can bear. The gap between what exists in the world and what a Caribbean patient can actually get is the real story, and it is a gap the region has the power to narrow.
An advance approved abroad does not reach a Caribbean patient on its own.
The opportunity, not only the gap

There is a business here as well as a burden. The Caribbean already sells medical travel, and a region that positions itself to offer advanced, non-invasive care has something to sell to its own diaspora and to the wider world, the same visitors who already come for the sea. The islands that invest in the equipment and the expertise turn a distant breakthrough into a local industry. The ones that do not watch their citizens fly abroad to be treated, and their money fly with them. The Ledger will keep a lens on the advances that change what care can do, and on the harder question of who in this region gets to reach them.

sources: Fox News; Focused Ultrasound Foundation; Parkinson's Foundation; Michael J. Fox Foundation. This article describes a medical development and is not medical advice.

headline: Africa's First Address Abroad, and What It Buys Barbados
stand: Afreximbank is spending 360 million dollars to build its first headquarters outside Africa, on a hill in Bridgetown. The building matters. What the deal says about Barbados matters more.

blocks.x: On Jemmotts Lane in St Michael, on ground that once held the first hospital built for formerly enslaved Barbadians in 1844, two twelve-storey towers are going up. When they are finished, they will be the Afreximbank African Trade Centre, the first headquarters the African Export-Import Bank has ever built outside the African continent. The bill is 360 million Barbados dollars, and the address is not Lagos, Cairo or Johannesburg. It is Bridgetown.

That single fact is worth sitting with. A pan-African financial institution with tens of billions on its balance sheet looked at the whole of the Americas and chose a country of fewer than three hundred thousand people to plant its first stake beyond home soil. Barbados did not win a factory or a call centre. It won an institution, and institutions do not leave.
What it means for the Caribbean

For the region, the centre is a door that swings both ways. Afreximbank exists to finance trade, and the whole point of a Caribbean headquarters is to move goods, services and capital between two places that history separated and geography still keeps apart. The building will house a regional headquarters for CARICOM, a hotel, conference and exhibition space, and what the bank calls a digital trade gateway. Read plainly, that is a physical desk in the Caribbean where an African exporter and a Caribbean buyer can be introduced, financed and settled without either of them routing the deal through London or New York first.

This is the part the region has to understand. The Caribbean has spent decades reaching the world through other people's banks and other people's rules, and paying a spread for the privilege every time. An institution like Afreximbank, sitting inside CARICOM and lending against Caribbean trade, is a second road out. It does not replace the traditional lines to the north. It gives the region somewhere else to turn when those lines narrow, and as the wider Ledger has argued, those lines are narrowing. A trade bank that treats the Caribbean and Africa as one market of roughly a hundred and fifty countries is a bigger market than any single island will ever negotiate alone.
Barbados did not win a factory. It won an institution, and institutions do not leave.
The build, and what it means for Barbados

Ground was broken in March 2025 on a schedule of about thirty months, which puts the handover in 2027. The project is now past the midpoint of that clock, and the towers on Jemmotts Lane have moved from drawings to structure. The immediate economics are straightforward. Construction is expected to carry roughly a thousand jobs, with close to fifty local small and medium firms working as subcontractors and suppliers, and around three hundred permanent positions once the centre opens. A Hyatt partnership is putting money into an urban transformation fund, and a further seven million dollars is pledged toward housing improvements in the surrounding neighbourhood.

Those numbers are real, but they are not the reason this matters to Barbados. The reason is what an anchor institution does to everything around it. A trade centre that hosts conferences and exhibitions fills hotel rooms and restaurants in the low season. A regional headquarters brings staff who rent, spend and bank on the island. A digital trade gateway gives Barbadian firms a front-row seat to African demand that most of their competitors elsewhere in the hemisphere cannot reach. The building is the visible part. The traffic it generates is the asset.
The Mottley method

None of this arrived by accident, and this is where the story becomes a study in how a small state punches above its weight. Prime Minister Mia Mottley has built a foreign policy that treats capital as something to be courted directly, and she has been consistent about it. Barbados helped bring CARICOM into Afreximbank as a member. It has hosted the AfriCaribbean Trade and Investment Forum. It has put the case, again and again, that the Caribbean and Africa should trade with each other rather than only with the powers that once traded them. The trade centre is the physical return on years of that argument.

Call it the Mottley method. It is the same approach that produced the Bridgetown Initiative on global finance and the same instinct that turns a state visit into a signed term sheet. A leader who can persuade an African institution to build its first overseas home on a Barbadian hill is a leader who has understood something many larger countries have not, that in a crowded world attention is capital, and a small country that is trusted, prepared and clear about what it wants can pull investment that its size alone would never command. Her quote at the groundbreaking said the plain thing well, that there could be no better use for this site.

The caution worth keeping is the one this paper always keeps. A groundbreaking is a promise, not a receipt. The value of the centre will be measured in 2028 and beyond, in the trade financed, the deals settled and the jobs that outlast the scaffolding. But the direction is set, and it is the right one. Barbados has traded a hospital site that once marked the region's pain for an institution that could help fund its future. That is not a bad exchange for a country that intends, in the Prime Minister's words, to reclaim its Atlantic destiny.

Details of the investment, the site and the groundbreaking were reported by the Barbados Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade and by Barbados Today. The Caribbean Ledger sets out the facts in its own words and adds its own read.

headline: The Windfall and the Waiting
stand: Guyana is the fastest-growing economy on earth, transformed by an offshore oil boom of historic scale. Six years in, the defining question is no longer whether the country is rich, but whether the wealth is reaching its people.

blocks.x: Along the East Bank of the Demerara River, past the hotels rising out of former cane fields and the queues of trucks bound for the shore bases, the scale of what has happened to Guyana becomes difficult to overstate. In 2019 this was one of the poorest countries in South America, an economy of sugar, rice, gold and bauxite worth a little over five billion dollars. Today, measured by the pace of its growth, it is the fastest-expanding economy on earth.

The engine of that change sits about 190 kilometres offshore, in a deepwater concession called the Stabroek Block operated by ExxonMobil with Hess and China's CNOOC. Since the first barrel was lifted in December 2019, production has climbed from roughly 75,000 barrels a day to around 900,000, and the government projects it will pass 1.3 million within a few years. For a nation of some 800,000 people, the arithmetic is staggering. It is also the source of the central question this newspaper begins its life by asking: whether a windfall of this size can be turned into lasting prosperity, or whether Guyana joins the long list of countries that struck oil and grew poorer for it.
A decade of numbers that break the chart

The clearest way to grasp the transformation is to look at the size of the economy itself. For most of the past decade Guyana's nominal output crept upward in the manner of a small agricultural state, from about 4.3 billion dollars in 2015 to 5.2 billion in 2019. Then oil arrived. Output more than doubled between 2021 and 2022, and by 2025 the economy was worth roughly 26 billion dollars, five times its pre-oil level. The International Monetary Fund recorded real growth of 43.6% in 2024, the highest of any economy it tracks, after an expansion of more than 60% in the first full year of production.

blocks.figt: An economy five times larger than it was before oil
blocks.fign: Nominal gross domestic product in current US dollars. Gold bars mark the years from first oil (December 2019) onward. Sources: International Monetary Fund World Economic Outlook; Bank of Guyana; Guyana Bureau of Statistics.

blocks.x: Growth of this order is not, on its own, a measure of national wellbeing. Nominal figures inflated by a single export can flatter a country while leaving most of its citizens where they were. The more demanding test is what the money is doing once it comes ashore, and for whom.
What the boom has meant for daily life

The evidence on ordinary lives is genuinely mixed, and honesty requires saying so. Public-sector wages have risen, a national programme has removed tuition at the University of Guyana, and the government has distributed cash transfers directly to households, including grants of 100,000 Guyana dollars per adult and payments tied to newborns and schoolchildren. Mortgage relief, part-time job schemes and subsidies on electricity and water have put money into pockets that were empty a decade ago. New roads, a bridge across the Demerara and a long-promised gas-to-shore project are under construction.

items.l: Barrels per day, 2026
Real GDP growth, 2024
Sovereign fund balance
Population

blocks.x: Yet the gains sit alongside strains that a rising average income conceals. The cost of living in Georgetown has climbed sharply, driven by rents and food prices in a capital suddenly full of oil workers and expatriate salaries. Households outside the boom's orbit, in the rural interior and among the Indigenous communities of the hinterland, report that prices reached them faster than wages did. Inequality, by most local accounts, has widened. A frequently cited estimate has placed the share of Guyanese living in poverty at more than half the population as the boom began, and while that baseline predates the largest transfers, it is a reminder of how far the country started behind.
The question is not whether Guyana is richer. It plainly is. The question is whether the wealth is being built into something that outlasts the oil.
How the wealth is being governed

Every petro-state eventually confronts the same problem: money arrives faster than the institutions built to manage it. Guyana's answer, at least on paper, is the Natural Resource Fund, a sovereign account established to hold the government's oil receipts and release them into the budget under a formula written into law. The fund held little more than a hundred million dollars in 2020. By 2025 its balance had grown to roughly 3.6 billion dollars, even as the government drew heavily on it to finance a national budget that reached about 1.38 trillion Guyana dollars.

blocks.figh: Natural Resource Fund · US$ billion, year-end balance
blocks.figt: A sovereign account filling faster than it is being drawn
blocks.fign: Approximate year-end balances of Guyana's Natural Resource Fund. Gold bars mark years in which large withdrawals were transferred to the national budget. Sources: Bank of Guyana; Ministry of Finance; Natural Resource Fund public reports.

blocks.x: The fund's design has drawn both credit and criticism. Supporters note that a rule-based mechanism is more than many resource economies managed at a comparable stage, and that withdrawals are reported and audited. Critics, including opposition figures and civil-society groups, argue that the 2021 rewrite of the fund's law concentrated too much discretion in the finance minister, weakened the independent oversight board, and allows so much of the inflow to be spent each year that little is genuinely being saved for the future. The debate is not academic. It is the difference between a fund that stabilises the country for a generation and one that functions as a second treasury drained in the political cycle.

The terms of the oil itself remain the most contested inheritance of all. The 2016 production-sharing agreement with the ExxonMobil group grants Guyana a royalty of 2% and a half share of profit oil after the companies recover their costs, with a cost-recovery ceiling that lets the operators reclaim up to three-quarters of production before profits are split. Independent analysts have argued the government captures a smaller share of the resource than it might have under a tougher contract, and a dispute over more than 200 million dollars in disputed expenses has run through the courts. Ministers counter that reopening the agreement would deter the investment now driving the boom, and that the priority is to spend well rather than to relitigate the past.

blocks.figh: Crude production · thousand barrels per day
blocks.figt: From first oil to nearly a million barrels a day in six years
blocks.fign: Approximate average daily crude production from the Stabroek Block, operated by ExxonMobil with Hess and CNOOC. 2026 figure is projected on installed and commissioning capacity. Sources: ExxonMobil operational updates; Guyana Department of Energy; industry reporting.

blocks.x: The test the next decade will set

Guyana has tried to write its own answer to the resource curse into policy. Its Low-Carbon Development Strategy pairs the oil economy with the sale of forest-carbon credits, and a landmark agreement is channelling hundreds of millions of dollars from the preservation of standing rainforest, a rare attempt to hedge a fossil-fuel windfall against the transition that will one day shrink it. Whether that ambition survives the gravitational pull of oil revenue is one of the more important experiments in development economics now under way anywhere.

The risks are the familiar ones. An exchange rate and a labour market bent around a single industry can hollow out farming and manufacturing, the classic Dutch disease. A young, English-speaking population is both an asset and a temptation to emigrate, and Guyana has long recorded one of the highest emigration rates in the hemisphere. And a border controversy with Venezuela over the Essequibo region, the very territory beneath which much of the oil lies, adds a geopolitical charge that no sovereign fund can insure against.

None of this settles the verdict, and it is too early to reach one. What can be said is that Guyana is being handed, in a single decade, a chance that most developing nations never receive: the capital to build schools, hospitals, power and institutions that would otherwise have taken generations to afford. The windfall is real. The waiting, for the roads to reach the villages, for the fund to be protected from the politics of the moment, for the growth to become something citizens can feel, is the harder part. The Caribbean Ledger begins its coverage of the region's defining economic story here, and intends to follow the money, patiently, all the way to shore.

sources: International Monetary Fund World Economic Outlook; Bank of Guyana; Guyana Bureau of Statistics; Ministry of Finance; Natural Resource Fund public reports; Inter-American Development Bank; ExxonMobil operational updates; Guyana Department of Energy; Stabroek News; Kaieteur News; Department of Public Information (DPI); Reuters; Bloomberg

headline: Massy Posts Higher FY2025 Profit As McLetchie Takes The Helm
stand: The Trinidad conglomerate grew earnings across a steadier 2025 even as a new chief executive and sharper portfolio focus reshaped the group.

blocks.x: A Diversified Model Holds Its Footing

Massy Holdings Limited, the Trinidad and Tobago based conglomerate that anchors much of the Caribbean's retail, energy and motoring trade, closed its 2025 financial year with steadier earnings and a fresh hand on the wheel. For the twelve months ended September 30, 2025, third-party revenue rose 3% to TT$15.83 billion, or roughly US$2.3 billion, while profit attributable to the parent's owners climbed 9% to TT$722.24 million.

Profit before tax advanced 4% to TT$1.14 billion, and operating profit after finance costs jumped 15% to TT$1.12 billion as the group trimmed finance costs by 12% to TT$256.76 million. Earnings per share reached TT$0.37, up from TT$0.33 a year earlier. Group President and CEO James McLetchie said the results demonstrate the resilience and strength of the group's diversified business model.
Three Portfolios, Uneven Weather

Massy now reports through three consolidated portfolios, and their fortunes diverged. The Integrated Retail Portfolio, spanning supermarkets and distribution across Trinidad, Barbados, Guyana and the OECS, delivered the standout, lifting profit about 14%. The Motors and Machines Portfolio added 2%, helped by resilient demand and strength in Colombia. The Gas Products Portfolio, long a hard-currency engine, saw profit slip about 8.5% on softer volumes, though management noted cost discipline protected profit before tax.

Financial services, folded into the wider group, deepened customer engagement by linking credit, digital payments and foreign-exchange offerings, part of a push to convert everyday transactions into recurring revenue across the islands.
New Leadership, Sharper Focus

The year also marked a leadership handover. McLetchie, formerly chief financial officer, became Group President and CEO on October 1, 2025, succeeding David Affonso, who retired after roughly 18 months in the role. Affonso had taken the top job in April 2024 following the early retirement of Gervase Warner, who led Massy for some 14 years. Ivette Zuniga stepped up as executive vice president and Group CFO, while Robert Riley chairs the board. Riley framed the agenda as advancing strategic clarity, ensuring disciplined growth, optimising capital allocation, and expanding hard currency earnings.

Hard currency remains the strategic thread. Since cross-listing on the Jamaica Stock Exchange in early 2022 to broaden its capital base, Massy has pressed a United States foothold, buying the Rowes supermarket chain in Jacksonville, Florida for US$47 million and adding a 170,000 square foot warehouse as a distribution hub. To fund the next leg, the group secured US$150 million in unsecured financing from IDB Invest, structured as a US$90 million ten-year term facility and a US$60 million revolving supply-chain line. Management has pointed the balance sheet toward a TT$25 billion revenue ambition by 2030, with further US and Latin American expansion in view.

For a house whose roots reach back more than a century in Port of Spain, the message from Massy's boardroom is continuity over spectacle: consolidate the core, defend the hard-currency earnings, and let disciplined capital, rather than headline acquisitions, carry the group into its second century.

sources: Trinidad and Tobago Newsday; Trinidad Express; Searchlight; Mayberry Investments; Jamaica Observer; Businessuite Online; Massy Group Annual Report 2025; Trinidad and Tobago Stock Exchange

headline: GraceKennedy Turns The Corner On Melissa As Recovery Takes Hold
stand: Jamaica's food and finance conglomerate has restored profit growth after last October's hurricane, with a food-led rebound and a widening push beyond home shores.

blocks.x: Recovery after the storm

GraceKennedy Limited, the Kingston-headquartered conglomerate that spans food distribution and financial services across the region and diaspora, has restored its earnings momentum. Half-year results to June 2026 show revenue of J$93.1 billion, up 4.6%, and net profit attributable to shareholders of J$4.75 billion, an 11.8% rise from J$4.25 billion a year earlier. Second-quarter net profit reached J$2.5 billion. Group Chief Executive Frank James told the market the company was seeing good signs of a recovery, with previously damaged sections back on stream and performing above expectations.

The rebound follows a punishing stretch. Hurricane Melissa struck western and central Jamaica in October 2025, driving insurance claims and disrupting manufacturing and logistics. Full-year 2025 revenue still climbed to J$177.8 billion, an increase of J$10.7 billion, but profit was squeezed: nine-month earnings to stockholders had already slipped roughly 8% to J$6.11 billion before the storm's full weight landed. James described core operations as intact but tested.
Food leads the rebound

The food division did the heavy lifting, contributing about two-thirds of group profit with pre-tax earnings near J$4.8 billion. International operations in the United Kingdom, United States and Canada strengthened, while the storm-damaged Grace Foods Processors meat plant in Westmoreland reopened early in the year and lifted output by the second quarter. Hi-Lo Food Stores and the domestic distribution arm anchored the local base. In December 2025 GraceKennedy bought out New Zealand's Fonterra from Dairy Industries (Jamaica), ending a 29-year joint venture and taking full ownership of the maker of Tastee cheese and Anchor powdered milk. James said the move positioned the group to scale the business and deepen its leadership in the dairy segment. Andrea Coy leads GraceKennedy Foods.
Financial group and remittances

GK Financial Group broadened the recovery. Banking and investments delivered pre-tax profit of J$995 million, up from J$600 million, powered by double-digit revenue and profit growth at First Global Bank. Insurance produced pre-tax profit of J$1.28 billion despite the Melissa claims wave. Money Services posted pre-tax profit of J$1.08 billion, holding up against a soft remittance market. GraceKennedy Money Services, the region's Western Union agent, has leaned on its GK One digital wallet, which integrates Western Union transfers, rolled out in Guyana and has now expanded into the Cayman Islands.
Vision 2030 and the next chapter

The results are the first full cycle under James, who became Group CEO in February 2025 after nearly two decades at the company, succeeding the retiring Don Wehby. He inherited an ambitious blueprint. Vision 2030 targets US$2.1 billion in revenue, US$250 million in pre-tax profit and 70% of revenue and profit generated outside Jamaica. The group passed the US$1 billion revenue mark in 2023, two years ahead of schedule, and is steering more of its growth toward the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom in food, alongside digital financial services across the Caribbean. With storm losses receding and the dairy acquisition bedding in, GraceKennedy enters its second century pressing that international case harder than ever.

sources: GraceKennedy Group press releases; Jamaica Gleaner, 'Grace turns the corner on Melissa', Aug 2 2026; Jamaica Gleaner, Nov 28 2025; Mayberry Investments; Jamaica Stock Exchange; BusinessuiteOnline

headline: Guyana Powers ANSA McAL To Record Half-Year Regional Growth
stand: The Trinidadian conglomerate's Guyana revenue jumped nearly 20%, cementing the oil economy as its fastest-growing market.

blocks.x: Guyana Becomes The Growth Engine

ANSA McAL, the Trinidad and Tobago conglomerate that spans beverages, banking, construction materials and services, has confirmed what its executives have argued for three years: Guyana is now the single fastest-growing market in its regional portfolio. In results released on August 8, the group reported that Guyana revenue climbed to TT$490 million in the first half of 2026, up 19.7% from TT$410 million in the same period a year earlier.

That expansion outpaced every other geography in which the group operates. Guyana's oil-driven boom, with GDP growth among the fastest on the planet, has pulled demand for beer, soft drinks, hardware and financial services sharply higher, and ANSA McAL has positioned its Guyanese subsidiaries to capture that lift.
Beverages And Banking Lead

Group-wide, ANSA McAL posted revenue of TT$3.790 billion for the half, a 3% increase, while profit before tax from continuing operations rose 25% to TT$401 million. Adjusted EBITDA reached TT$751 million, up 8%, and earnings per share grew 50% to TT$1.50. The company said the beverage and financial services sectors delivered its strongest contributions, with services also aided by gains from strategic asset sales.

Beverages are central to the Guyana story. The group's local brewer, Guyana Breweries Inc, has been scaling production to meet a consumer market swelling with oil-sector wages, while ANSA McAL's distribution and trading arms have widened their reach across Georgetown and the coast. In October 2025 the group also agreed to stock Guyanese-made products across its supermarket network, deepening its local sourcing footprint.
A Half-Billion-Dollar War Chest

The expansion is backed by fresh capital. ANSA McAL has secured a financing partnership of up to US$500 million with IDB Invest, the private-sector arm of the Inter-American Development Bank, a commitment the group describes as the largest of its kind in the Caribbean. The facility is earmarked for the group's investment programme, regional expansion and sustainability initiatives, giving it firepower to keep building out in Guyana and beyond.

Balance-sheet discipline has accompanied the growth. The group repaid TT$683 million of debt during the half, cutting its gearing ratio to 19.6% from 23.9% at the close of 2025. Regional ratings agency CariCRIS has assigned the company a CariAA regional-scale rating with a stable outlook.
Confidence Across The Region

Group Chairman A. Norman Sabga framed the performance as validation of a long-run strategy. The first half of 2026 demonstrates the resilience of the Group and continued market confidence in ANSA McAL's strategic direction, he said, adding that the company's financial strength, diversification, and disciplined execution underpin its ability to navigate uncertainty while creating long-term value for stakeholders across the region.

The trajectory extends a run that began well before the current boom peaked. ANSA McAL grew group profits 13.6% in full-year 2024 as its Guyana bet started to pay off. With oil production still ramping and a US$500 million credit line at its back, the conglomerate has made clear that its regional growth story now runs through Georgetown.

sources: Kaieteur News, Aug 8 2026; News Source Guyana; ANSA McAL Group results; Stabroek News, Mar 23 2025; Stabroek News, Oct 18 2025; Trinidad Express

headline: CARICOM Extends Its Food Security Drive To 2030
stand: The region missed its 2025 deadline to cut food imports by a quarter, but production is up and the target now runs to 2030.

blocks.x: A regional bill, rewritten

CARICOM's signature agriculture campaign, the 25 by 2025 initiative, set out to cut the region's food import bill by 25% by the end of 2025. That deadline has passed without the full target met. On February 21, 2025, Guyana's President Dr. Irfaan Ali announced that Heads of Government had expanded and extended the initiative to 2030, reframing it around a broader push for a resilient, sustainable and competitive regional food system. The import bill the effort targets stands at more than US$6 billion a year.
What the numbers show

The extension is not a retreat from progress. Ali, who serves as CARICOM's Lead Head of Government for Agriculture and Food Security, has cited roughly a 24% increase in food production across the region between 2022 and late 2024. Earlier data he presented to the 47th Heads of Government meeting in Grenada in July 2024 pointed to a 12% decline in food imports in real terms, worth about US$250 million, and a CARICOM and World Food Programme survey from April 2024 recording a drop in food insecurity to 17% of the surveyed population.

Officials have been candid that external shocks slowed the timeline. Hurricane Beryl caused agricultural damage estimated at about US$150 million in 2024, and leaders have pointed to global trade uncertainty and supply chain disruption as further drags on the schedule.
Guyana at the center

Guyana has positioned itself as the production engine of the strategy. Its 2026 national agriculture budget reached a record GY$104.6 billion, roughly US$500 million, up sharply from GY$18.4 billion in 2020. Agriculture Minister Zulfikar Mustapha chairs the CARICOM Ministerial Task Force on Agriculture. The country has moved beyond planning into shipments, sending cassava chips and mango pulp to Antigua and corn, soya and poultry to Barbados, with Ali describing Guyana as self-sufficient across key food categories and pressing an ambition to become the Caribbean's food capital.
The stubborn barriers

The obstacles the region must still clear are structural rather than agronomic. CARICOM's own framing identifies three: inadequate regional air and sea transportation for moving produce between islands, the difficulty of financing and insuring farmers, and persistent trade barriers between member states. To address the financing gap, the region has stood up a Caribbean Food Systems Investment Initiative and a US$100 million regional agriculture fund, and launched the Regional Economic Agri-Insurance Programme in July 2024. The European Union has committed a 19 million euro programme to strengthen Caribbean agri-food systems. Analysts continue to argue that without a unified intra-regional transport strategy, produce grown in surplus in one territory cannot reliably reach shortage markets in another.
On target, on a longer clock

By May 2026, Ali described the initiative as on target, reporting that the region had reached 88% of its production goal for non-traditional crops. The recalibration to 2030 gives CARICOM room to convert rising output into a durable cut in dependence on imported food. The measure of success is no longer a single date. It is whether the region can pair record production with the transport, finance and trade reforms that turn harvests into full plates across the Caribbean.

sources: CARICOM Secretariat; Kaieteur News, May 7 2026; ReliefWeb, CARICOM AGRI Investment Forum; Department of Public Information Guyana

headline: Off The Lists, Not Off The Hook On Correspondent Banking
stand: The region has cleared FATF and EU watchlists, but the correspondent banking squeeze that de-risking set in motion has not eased.

blocks.x: A quiet run of delistings

The last two years handed the Caribbean a rare sequence of good news on financial reputation. On February 23, 2024, the Financial Action Task Force removed Barbados from its list of jurisdictions under increased monitoring, the so-called grey list, following an on-site assessment earlier that month. Jamaica followed at the FATF plenary of June 26 to 28, 2024, ending a listing that had run since 2020. Both governments cast the exits as proof that costly reform programs had worked.
Brussels moves in step

The European Union then aligned its own regime. On June 10, 2025, the European Commission published a revised list of high-risk third countries for money laundering and terrorist financing that delisted Barbados, Jamaica and Panama, alongside Gibraltar, the United Arab Emirates and others. For Bridgetown and Kingston, that closed a painful loop: EU and United Kingdom blacklisting had followed directly from the FATF listings, and delisting reversed the chain.
Haiti stays under watch

The regional picture is not uniform. Haiti remains under FATF increased monitoring, one of the few Caribbean states still identified for strategic deficiencies. At its October 24, 2025 plenary the FATF removed Burkina Faso, Mozambique, Nigeria and South Africa and added no new jurisdictions, leaving only the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, Iran and Myanmar on the highest-risk call-for-action list. The Caribbean is no longer a headline concern for the standard-setters, but the reputational scar tissue remains.
The deeper problem outlasts the lists

Delisting does not restore what de-risking took away. The core grievance across CARICOM is the retreat of global banks from correspondent relationships, the account links that let local banks clear US dollars and process cross-border payments. The International Monetary Fund has documented the Caribbean as among the regions hardest hit by this withdrawal, with small economies losing the very connections that trade, remittances and tourism depend on. Where relationships survived, they often came with higher fees and heavier compliance demands that erode already thin banking margins.
A region making its own case

The policy response has been to organize rather than wait. De-risking has stayed high on the agenda of the Caribbean Financial Action Task Force, the regional FATF-style body, which continues to press that wholesale exit from the region is disproportionate to actual risk. The Caribbean Development Bank has funded work aimed at preventing further loss of correspondent banking relationships, and CARICOM heads have repeatedly carried the argument to Washington and Brussels that de-risking treats compliant institutions as collateral damage. The framing regional leaders now favor is blunt: correspondent banking access should be treated as something close to a public good, not a discretionary commercial choice.
What the wins are worth

The delistings matter because they remove an excuse. A global bank can no longer point to a FATF or EU listing to justify cutting a Barbadian or Jamaican counterpart loose. But they do not compel any bank to open or keep an account, and that gap is where the region's exposure still lives. The unfinished work is turning hard-won clean status into durable access, so that clearing a watchlist buys more than a press release.

sources: FATF Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring, 2024-2025; Central Bank of Barbados; Bank of Jamaica; European Commission; IMF, Loss of Correspondent Banking Relationships in the Caribbean; CARICOM; Atlantic Council

headline: Record arrivals collide with a deepening Caribbean staffing crunch
stand: As the region shatters visitor records, hotels and restaurants cannot find enough workers to serve them.

blocks.x: The paradox of a full house

The Caribbean has never been busier, and it has never been shorter of the people who make the busyness work. International tourist arrivals reached 34.2 million in 2024, a 6.1% rise over 2023 and 6.9% above the pre-pandemic peak of 2019, according to the Caribbean Tourism Organization. Cruise passenger visits climbed even faster, to 33.7 million, up 10.3%. The CTO expects overnight arrivals to touch 35 million in 2025. Behind those numbers sits an uncomfortable truth managers across the region now say openly: the guests are arriving faster than the workforce can grow.
A sector that carries the region

Travel and tourism is not a side business for the Caribbean; it is the payroll. The World Bank estimates the sector contributed 11.4% of regional GDP in 2023 and supported more than 2.75 million jobs, roughly 15.1% of all regional employment. In some economies the dependence is far heavier. In St. Lucia, 55% of workers aged 15 to 24 are employed in tourism. Women make up between 57 and 70% of the accommodation and food services workforce, well above the global average. When staffing tightens, it is these workers and their communities who feel it first.
Where the gaps are widest

Curacao offers a sharp illustration. Tourism there accounts for 48% of GDP and employs over 20,000 people, and the local hospitality association CHATA estimates the island needs 2,000 to 3,000 additional workers over the next two years as more than 1,000 new hotel and apartment units come online. Shortages are most acute among cooks, servers, bartenders, front office staff and housekeeping. The number of students and job seekers simply does not match the growth rate of our industry, CHATA chief executive Anuschka Cova said. Board chair Mimi Luttge argued for a dual approach: We must pursue a dual strategy, actively recruit local talent while also temporarily importing foreign workers.
Wages, quality and the retention problem

The strain is not only about headcount. World Bank analysis finds tourism jobs lag industry and other services on a composite measure of earnings, benefits, stability and working conditions, with high turnover and few long-term career pathways. Seasonality and exposure to external shocks make the work less stable, and women consistently record lower job quality than men in the sector. Hotel economics, meanwhile, are strong: regional occupancy averaged 66.6% in 2024 and the average daily rate reached US$437.02, up 4.2%. The question regional leaders increasingly ask is why buoyant room rates have not translated into stickier, better-paid careers.
A global squeeze, felt locally

The pressure is not unique to the Caribbean. The World Travel and Tourism Council projects a global hospitality workforce shortfall of 8.6 million by 2035, about 18% below required levels, and industry surveys rank talent recruitment and retention as the number one challenge at 52%. For the Caribbean, the WTTC sees the sector adding 1.34 million jobs over the coming decade. Filling them will require training pipelines, salary benchmarking and immigration policy moving in step. Despite geopolitical uncertainty and global economic challenges, our sector has shown remarkable resilience, CTO Secretary-General Dona Regis-Prosper said. Resilience, the region is learning, still runs on people.

sources: Caribbean Tourism Organization / OneCaribbean.org; Caribbean Hotel and Tourism Association; Curacao Hospitality and Tourism Association (CHATA); World Bank Blogs; World Travel & Tourism Council

headline: Remote-work visas reshape Caribbean labour and housing markets
stand: Six years after Barbados opened the door to laptop workers, the region is counting the foreign exchange and reckoning with the rents.

blocks.x: A pandemic experiment becomes policy

When Prime Minister Mia Mottley launched the Barbados Welcome Stamp in mid-2020, the offer was simple: bring your foreign salary, live on the island for a year, and pay tax at home rather than in Bridgetown. The idea spread fast across a region whose tourism receipts had collapsed. Six years on, at least eight jurisdictions run remote-work visa schemes, and the question has shifted from whether nomads will come to what they leave behind.

Barbados remains the reference case. Government figures put total Welcome Stamp applications at more than 8,000, with roughly 2,900 approved and about 1,000 holders actually arriving to activate the visa. The programme drew applicants from 136 nationalities, led by the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and Nigeria, and generated at least US$6 million in foreign exchange across its first three years from application fees alone. The standard fee is US$2,000 for an individual and US$3,000 for a family, for twelve months.
Eight schemes, eight price tags

The regional menu is now varied. Antigua and Barbuda's Nomad Digital Residence runs two years and requires proof of US$50,000 in annual income, with fees from US$1,500. Montserrat's Remote Workers Programme sets a US$70,000 income bar; Dominica markets its Work In Nature visa around eco-tourism; Anguilla, Curacao and the Cayman Islands each pitch to different tiers of earner, with Cayman's Global Citizen Concierge Programme aimed squarely at the six-figure end, requiring income between US$100,000 and US$180,000.

The common logic is foreign-currency inflow without a work permit that competes for local jobs. Nomads are barred from taking domestic employment, spending instead on rent, restaurants, transport and services. For small open economies that import most of what they consume, that hard currency is the point, and central banks watch it closely.
The housing reckoning

The cost is showing up in the property market. Remote workers earning metropolitan salaries can outbid residents for the same short-term rentals, and in desirable coastal districts the pressure on prices has become a live political issue. Longer visas intensify the strain: a two-year permit is a two-year housing commitment in markets that were already tight before the first laptop arrived. Local labour, meanwhile, sees demand rise in hospitality and property management but little movement in wages, and workers priced out of neighbourhoods they have long lived in are the sharper grievance.
Tightening, not retreating

The clearest warning came from Bermuda, which ended its Work From Bermuda residential certificate in February 2025 after concluding the scheme no longer served the island's interests. Elsewhere the direction is not withdrawal but discipline: governments increasingly favour stable, rule-following residents over serial short-stayers, tightening income proofs, health-insurance and background checks, and weighing whether the revenue justifies the pressure on housing.

The pan-Caribbean lesson from six years of experimentation is that a remote-work visa is not free money. It is a trade: durable foreign exchange and off-season spending against the risk of pricing residents out of their own communities. The jurisdictions likely to keep these programmes are those that show a visible economic benefit while holding the line on rents, and that treat the digital nomad as a guest of the economy rather than a substitute for developing it.

sources: Barbados Ministry of Tourism, Welcome Stamp Statistics; Barbados Today, Oct 25 2025; Barbados Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade; Caribbean & Co.; The Rio Times; Appleby; Government of Bermuda

headline: How Caribbean Cuisine Became An Export And A Soft-Power Asset
stand: From London dining rooms chasing a first star to a rum trade worth billions, the region's kitchens are now a serious economy.

blocks.x: For decades the region's food traveled as memory: a patty at a diaspora bakery, a bottle of pepper sauce in a suitcase. In 2025 and 2026 it travels as commerce and as culture, and the numbers are beginning to match the ambition. Across London, Kingston and the tourism boards, Caribbean cooking is being treated less as holiday nostalgia and more as an asset with balance-sheet value.
The London test kitchen

No Caribbean restaurant in London has yet won a Michelin star, but a cohort is openly working toward one. Bloomberg reported in May 2025 on chefs including Nathaniel Mortley, whose refined room 2210 in Herne Hill drew immediate crowds, alongside Keshia Sakarah's residency at The Pilgrm and Dom Taylor's The Good Front Room. Their reference point is close to home: West African peers Chishuru and Akoko earned first stars in 2024, and Ikoyi now holds two. The message is that a food long read as casual can command fine-dining recognition.
Awards and festivals as infrastructure

Recognition is now being built at home rather than borrowed from abroad. The second annual Caribbean Culinary Impact Awards, staged by Best Dressed Plate and reported in December 2025, honored chefs across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom and the region, naming the Grenada Tourism Authority Best Caribbean Culinary Destination and giving Jamaica twelve honors, among them chefs Brian Lumley and Lonnie Murdock. The Jamaica Food and Drink Festival, which marked its tenth anniversary in November 2024, again took a regional title in October 2025 after earlier Caribbean festival honors from the World Culinary Awards.
Rum, the proven export

If restaurants are the emerging story, rum is the established one. Industry estimates put Caribbean rum exports near 1.8 billion US dollars a year, with the United States taking roughly 42% of shipments, the European Union about 22% and the United Kingdom near 18%, and forecasts pointing toward 2.6 billion by 2030 on the strength of premiumization. Super-premium bottlings are the fastest-moving segment. The 2025 Caribbean Rum Awards, covered by Forbes in December, underscored how a category once sold on price is now sold on provenance, from Barbados to Jamaica's estate distilleries.

That premium logic increasingly extends to the plate. Jerk, roti, pepperpot and estate rum are being marketed together as a single origin story, and consumers are paying for authenticity rather than a generic tropical theme. Where a jerk stand once competed on cost, the region's producers and chefs now compete on heritage, technique and place.
Food as the new tourism pitch

For tourism ministries this is a rare form of leverage. A dish cannot be relocated to a cheaper coastline, and a festival keeps visitor spending onshore and in local kitchens. Grenada's culinary-destination recognition, Jamaica's festival economy and the diaspora dining rooms of London and Toronto now function as one connected marketing engine. Caribbean cuisine has become a genuine instrument of influence, carrying the region's name into rooms that visa lines and advertising budgets rarely reach, and turning flavor into durable economic and cultural capital.

sources: Bloomberg, May 22 2025; Jamaica Observer, Dec 22 2025; Jamaica Observer, Oct 24 2025; Forbes, Mar 6 2025; Forbes, Dec 7 2025; Hope Research Group

headline: How the CPL Turned Cricket Into a Caribbean Economic Engine
stand: A sponsor-backed T20 league now moves tourists, jobs and a billion screens across the region every August.

blocks.x: A league built on partners, not just prize money

When the Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League bowls its first ball of the 2026 season on August 7, running through to September 20, it does so as the most commercially mature sporting property the region has produced. The economics are now the story as much as the cricket. On September 24, 2025, Republic Bank, the largest financial institution in the English-speaking Caribbean, renewed its title sponsorship for a further three years, deepening a relationship that began as official banking partner in 2016 and became the naming rights deal in 2023. Crucially, the renewal also covers the Women's CPL and the bank's Five for Fun grassroots youth programme, tying the franchise's growth to a single long-term backer.
The audience that anchors the valuation

Sponsors are buying reach, and the numbers justify the spend. CPL 2024 drew a combined broadcast and digital audience of 1.13 billion, a 32% jump on 2023, with notable growth in India, the United States and the Caribbean itself. The 2025 edition pushed the figure to 1.17 billion. Chief executive Pete Russell has called crossing the billion-viewer threshold a long-standing goal, and it reframes the league from a regional diversion into a genuine global media asset. That audience underpins an estimated US$225.4 million in economic impact generated across the Caribbean in 2024.

For host governments, the appeal is that this reach converts into arrivals. The league now commissions island-by-island impact studies, and they read like tourism-board business cases rather than sports reports.
What a fortnight of cricket puts on the ground

Antigua and Barbuda's 2025 hosting delivered a US$19.5 million total impact, split between US$10.7 million in direct economic activity and US$8.8 million in international media value. The matches drew 23,553 fans, including 1,733 international visitors who stayed an average of 4.5 nights and spent roughly US$3,100 each, while 169 jobs were created for the event. St Kitts and Nevis reported a near-identical US$19.9 million from five matches at Warner Park, with more than 3,000 international visitors and 94 jobs, lifting the league's cumulative investment in the twin-island federation to US$13.6 million over a decade.

The pattern is deliberate. By spreading fixtures across Trinidad, Guyana, Barbados, St Lucia, St Kitts, Antigua and a returning Jamaica, the CPL functions as a rotating stimulus package, filling hotel rooms in the shoulder season and buying global airtime for destinations that could never afford it outright.
The women's game as the next growth lever

The clearest signal of confidence is expansion. The Massy Women's CPL, launched in 2022 with three sides, adds a fourth for 2026 as the Jamaica Empress join Barbados Royals, Guyana Amazon Warriors and Trinbago Knight Riders, with the short tournament staged in Barbados from September 5 to 17. Organisers have gone further, stating plans to welcome teams from outside the Caribbean in 2027 and build a genuinely global women's competition.

That ambition captures the wider bet. The CPL has stopped selling itself as a summer festival and started operating as regional infrastructure, an August engine that recruits sponsors, exports the Caribbean brand to a billion screens, and banks the visitor spending at home. For an economy of small islands, few assets do all three at once.

sources: CPL T20; cricexec.com; associatestimes.com; Jamaica Gleaner; Female Cricket; Republic Bank (republictt.com)

headline: Stop Waiting on Washington to Fix Our Banking Pipes
stand: The Caribbean must build its own payments backbone and pooled compliance utilities instead of pleading with global banks to keep us connected.

blocks.x: For most of my career in Caribbean banking, correspondent relationships were plumbing. You never thought about the pipes until they burst. Now they are bursting, and we keep waiting for someone in Washington or London to fix them for us. That wait is the mistake.

De-risking is not a rumor. When global banks decided that small Caribbean markets were more compliance trouble than they were worth, they simply withdrew. The Caribbean Association of Banks found in a 2017 survey that twenty-one of its twenty-three member banks had lost at least one correspondent banking relationship. Between 2011 and 2020, Belize, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Dominica, The Bahamas and Jamaica each saw such relationships fall by more than forty percent. These are the wires that let a hotel accept a foreign card, a diaspora nurse send money home, a distributor pay for imported medicine.

The human stakes are not abstract. In Jamaica, remittances are worth roughly a fifth of national output, and every severed relationship pushes those flows toward fewer, costlier channels, or underground entirely. Concentration is its own danger. When a whole economy routes its dollars through one or two remaining counterparties, the withdrawal of a single bank stops being an inconvenience and becomes a national emergency.
The habit we must break

Our reflex has been to plead. Prime Minister Mia Mottley took the case to the United States Congress in 2022, and she was right to. But diplomacy that asks large banks to be more patient with us is, by design, a posture of dependence. It treats our access to the financial system as a favor to be renewed rather than infrastructure we control. A region that earns its own foreign exchange should not have to petition for the right to move it.

The alternative is finally taking shape. Caribbean central banks have adopted the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System model, and are building the CARICOM Payment and Settlement System, or CAPSS, with technical support from Afreximbank. In February 2025 the central banks of Barbados and The Bahamas completed a successful pilot, settling cross-border transactions in local currency. As Barbados Governor Kevin Greenidge put it, when trade clears regionally you need fewer United States dollars for daily activity, freeing scarce hard currency for the things only dollars can buy.
What we actually control

CAPSS is the settlement backbone. The other half of the answer is compliance. De-risking happened partly because our small banks could not individually satisfy the anti money laundering expectations of correspondents many times their size. So pool the function. A shared regional compliance utility, screening transactions and maintaining common standards across jurisdictions, would give a global bank one credible counterparty to trust instead of a dozen it cannot afford to vet. We should fund it together and staff it with our own expertise.

I want to be fair to the doubters. Regional cooperation in the Caribbean has a long record of promising and stalling, and sovereignty over payments is politically delicate. A regional system cannot yet clear a dollar in New York, so correspondent relationships will remain necessary for some time. Building shared infrastructure is expensive for economies already stretched thin. These are reasons to design carefully, not reasons to do nothing.

Because the deeper risk is passivity. If we treat de-risking as weather, something that happens to us, we will keep losing pipes one by one until the room floods. If we treat it as architecture, something we can build, we change the terms. The Caribbean will not secure its place in global finance by being a more agreeable customer. We secure it by owning infrastructure that makes us worth connecting to.

sources: Caribbean Association of Banks 2017 survey, via Atlantic Council; IMF Working Paper WP/17/209; testimony of PM Mia Mottley, US House Financial Services Committee, September 2022; Trinidad Express, CAPSS coverage; PAPSS statement on CARICOM adoption; Central Bank of Barbados Governor Kevin Greenidge remarks

headline: The Oil Is Guyana's, But the Opportunity Belongs to Us All
stand: Guyana's oil boom is the Caribbean's best chance in a generation to build a single, self-reliant economy, and squandering it on one nation's balance sheet would be a regional failure.

blocks.x: In thirty years around Caribbean banking, I learned to distrust booms. I watched sugar, bauxite and tourism each promise permanence and each deliver a cycle. So I approach Guyana's oil with the caution of a former managing director who has seen balance sheets flatter and then betray small economies. And yet I cannot remember a chance like this one, and I do not think we get another.

The scale is not speculative. Guyana's economy grew 43.6% in 2024, according to its Bureau of Statistics, ranking it among the fastest-growing economies in the world. Offshore output from the ExxonMobil-led Stabroek Block, worked alongside Hess and CNOOC, has climbed past 900,000 barrels a day, and 2026 volumes are running ahead of forecast. The country's Natural Resource Fund, its sovereign wealth vehicle, crossed four billion United States dollars for the first time this year.
A regional windfall, not a national one

Here is my position. This money should be treated as capital, not as one nation's lucky cash. The Caribbean already owns the instrument to do it. The CARICOM Single Market and Economy, the CSME, was built precisely so that goods, capital, skills and enterprise could move across our borders as if the region were one market. For decades it has moved too slowly. A patient, Guyana-anchored pool of investment in regional ports, energy, agriculture and manufacturing could give the single market the momentum that forty years of communiques never did.

Food is the obvious place to start. CARICOM imports billions of dollars in food each year, an absurd dependency for fertile islands. The 25 by 2025 initiative, championed by Guyana's President Irfaan Ali and now extended toward 2030, aims to cut that regional food bill by a quarter. Guyana has the land and now the money; its neighbours have the markets and the mouths. Financing regional agriculture is not charity. It is the highest-return investment on offer, and it retires a shared vulnerability.
The risks deserve an honest hearing

I will not pretend the objections are trivial. Dutch disease is real; oil money can inflate a currency and hollow out the farming and manufacturing that integration is meant to build. Governance is real; a sovereign fund is only as sound as the institutions that guard it, and Guyana's are young. And sovereignty is real; no Guyanese voter elected a government to underwrite the region, and it is fair to ask why Georgetown should carry Kingston or Bridgetown.

But these arguments cut both ways. The surest defence against Dutch disease is to invest the windfall in productive capacity outside the oil sector, and a regional market is the widest field in which to do it. The surest defence against a governance failure is to bind the fund to transparent, cross-border projects that many eyes are watching. And the sovereignty question answers itself once you count the return: a stable, integrated, food-secure region is a safer and richer neighbourhood for Guyana than a resentful ring of stagnating states. Integration is not a gift Guyana gives; it is a hedge Guyana buys.

So my argument to my fellow Caribbean readers, and to Georgetown, is simple. The oil is finite and Guyana's alone. The prosperity it could seed is renewable and could be ours together. I have spent an entire career waiting for the capital to make the single market real. It has arrived. Let us not record, a generation from now, that the Caribbean's richest decade was also its most divided.

sources: IMF 2025 Article IV Consultation with Guyana; Guyana Bureau of Statistics (2024 GDP growth 43.6%); ExxonMobil Stabroek Block updates; CARICOM 25 by 2025 Food Security Initiative; Guyana Natural Resource Fund reporting via OilNOW

headline: Butterfield's $1.8 Billion CIBC Caribbean Deal Redraws Regional Banking
stand: Bermuda's Butterfield is buying control of CIBC Caribbean, ending a Canadian era and creating a $29 billion regional lender now awaiting regulators across ten jurisdictions.

blocks.x: The largest bank deal in the region's history

The Canadian era in Caribbean banking is ending. In an agreement announced on May 28, The Bank of N.T. Butterfield & Son, the Bermuda-based lender, will acquire control of CIBC Caribbean in a transaction valued at roughly $1.8 billion, the biggest banking deal the region has seen. Butterfield is buying the 91.7% stake held by Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, the parent that has anchored the franchise since it was assembled two decades ago. Nearly three months on, the deal has moved from headline to hard work, with regulators across the region now holding the timetable.

The structure is telling. Of the total consideration, about 61%, or roughly $1.09 billion, is cash, with the balance of some $703 million paid in Butterfield shares. That mix leaves CIBC as a continuing shareholder of about 22% in the enlarged group, with two seats on Butterfield's board and standstill and lockup terms attached. Butterfield also intends a mandatory offer for the remaining 8.3% minority. The combined institution would hold approximately $29 billion in total assets, with a pro forma common equity tier one ratio above 12%, backed by $700 million of committed subordinated debt financing.
Canada's long retreat, completed

The sale closes a chapter that began in 2002, when the Caribbean operations of Barclays and CIBC merged to form FirstCaribbean International Bank. CIBC took majority control in 2006 and rebranded the business CIBC Caribbean in early 2024. Today it spans ten countries, employs roughly 2,700 people and runs about 41 branches and offices, with the bulk of earnings drawn from Barbados, the Bahamas and the Cayman Islands.

CIBC's exit follows a broader Canadian and international withdrawal from Caribbean retail banking. Scotiabank sold operations across nine regional markets to Trinidad's Republic Financial Holdings in an earlier round of consolidation, and Royal Bank of Canada has pared its footprint over the past decade. Rising compliance costs, correspondent banking and de-risking pressures, and the pull of higher returns in North America have made scale in the islands harder to justify for the big Canadian lenders. CIBC's chief executive, Harry Culham, framed the move as a step to refocus capital on the bank's core North American market while praising the Caribbean team's client franchise.
A wealth manager reaching for scale

For Butterfield the logic runs the other way. Chairman and chief executive Michael Collins cast the acquisition as combining two complementary institutions and positioning the group as a leading independent bank and wealth manager across international financial centres. The deal roughly reshapes Butterfield from a Bermuda and Channel Islands specialist into a Caribbean-wide franchise. Management is guiding to double-digit earnings accretion in the first full year and about $49 million in annual cost savings once fully phased by 2030.
Regulators hold the keys

Completion is targeted for the first half of 2027 and remains subject to regulatory clearance and customary conditions. That is no formality. Approvals will be required from central banks and supervisors across the ten markets where the bank operates, a patchwork that has slowed prior regional transactions. Butterfield intends to keep its primary listings on the New York Stock Exchange and the Bermuda Stock Exchange while pursuing secondary listings in Barbados, the Bahamas and Trinidad and Tobago, a signal that it wants regional investors and depositors invested in the outcome.

The stakes reach beyond two balance sheets. A durable, well-capitalised owner could steady a franchise central to trade, tourism and cross-border payments in several small economies. The question supervisors will weigh is whether concentrating so much of the region's banking in a shrinking set of hands strengthens resilience or narrows competition. Their answers, market by market, will determine when this deal actually closes.

sources: Butterfield Group official release (butterfieldgroup.com); Business Wire; CIBC investor communications; Private Banker International; Jamaica Gleaner; Jamaica Observer; The Royal Gazette; Global Finance Magazine; The Caribbean Council; Republic Bank news releases

headline: Free Movement Widens As Four States Open Their Borders
stand: A subset of CARICOM members has moved from skilled-worker mobility to full free movement, and the region's private sector is pressing the rest to follow.

blocks.x: From skilled certificates to full mobility

For most of the CARICOM Single Market and Economy's life, the right to work across borders belonged to a defined class of people. Under the skilled-national regime, twelve categories of workers, expanded over years from a narrow professional list to include artisans, agricultural workers and other wage earners, could seek employment in another member state without a work permit once they held a CARICOM Skilled National certificate. That framework moved professionals, but it left large parts of the labour force outside the market.

That ceiling is now lifting for a group of countries. On 1 October 2025, Barbados, Belize, Dominica, and St. Vincent and the Grenadines began implementing full free movement, allowing nationals of the four to travel among them to reside, work and remain indefinitely, rather than for the six-month window that governed casual entry before.
The enhanced cooperation route

The legal vehicle is the Enhanced Cooperation Protocol to the Revised Treaty of Chaguaramas, which permits a group of at least three member states to press ahead with deeper integration without waiting for full consensus. That mechanism traces back to the 45th Regular Meeting of the Conference of Heads of Government in July 2023, when leaders committed to free movement of all categories of nationals to live and work in the Community. Haiti received a derogation from the arrangement given its circumstances.

The new status carries contingent rights that the older regime did not guarantee, including access to emergency and primary health care and to public primary and secondary education. Participating states have paired the opening with registration systems, security screening through IMPACS and the Advance Passenger Information System, and a complaints procedure meant to be reviewed within a fixed short window.
Who joins next

The pioneering four are no longer expected to remain alone. At the 51st Regular Meeting of the Conference of Heads of Government, held in Gros Islet, Saint Lucia in July 2026, leaders welcomed notification from Grenada and Saint Lucia that they are actively taking steps to participate in full free movement. Montserrat, an associate territory, signalled that it is preparing to accede to the Revised Treaty of Chaguaramas. The larger economies, including Trinidad and Tobago and Jamaica, have not yet entered the enhanced-cooperation group, and their nationals continue to move under the existing skilled-worker regime.
What it means for business

For employers, the shift addresses a constraint that regional business has identified for years. The CARICOM Private Sector Organisation welcomed the October opening and urged remaining states to follow, arguing that labour-mobility limits have held back construction, agriculture, tourism and services. CPSO Chairman Gervase Warner tied the case to opportunities in fast-growing markets such as Guyana and Jamaica, calling swift access to skilled and semi-skilled labour an essential condition for private-sector-led expansion. Chief Executive Dr. Patrick Antoine noted shortages affecting crops including sugar, cocoa and banana, linking freer labour to the region's food-security targets.

The practical test now is uniformity. A single market that operates full mobility in four states, a skilled-worker regime in the rest, and pending accessions elsewhere asks firms to navigate more than one rulebook at once. Whether the enhanced-cooperation core widens quickly, or hardens into a two-speed CSME, will shape hiring, service delivery and investment decisions across the Community over the coming year.

sources: CARICOM Secretariat; Communique of the 45th Regular Meeting of the Conference of Heads of Government (July 2023); Communique of the 51st Regular Meeting of the Conference of Heads of Government, Saint Lucia (July 2026); CARICOM Private Sector Organisation (CPSO) statement, Gervase Warner and Dr. Patrick Antoine; Government of Barbados Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade FAQs on Enhanced Cooperation in Free Movement

headline: Caribbean data protection regimes arrive unevenly as compliance costs mount
stand: From Bermuda to Kingston, privacy statutes are taking effect at different speeds, leaving regional banks and fintechs to manage a patchwork of obligations.

blocks.x: A region legislating privacy at different speeds

Across the Caribbean, governments have spent the past two years converting long-dormant data protection statutes into live regulatory regimes. The direction of travel is unmistakable, but the pace is not uniform. Some jurisdictions now have fully operational commissioners with enforcement powers, while others have passed laws that remain only partly proclaimed, leaving businesses to prepare for obligations whose start dates keep shifting.
Bermuda and the offshore centres move first

Bermuda has set the regional benchmark. Its Personal Information Protection Act, known as PIPA, came into full effect on January 1, 2025, giving the Office of the Privacy Commissioner supervisory authority over how organisations collect and use personal information. The Cayman Islands has run an operational regime for several years under its Data Protection Act, enforced by the Ombudsman, while Barbados brought its Data Protection Act into force with a dedicated Data Protection Commissioner. For the offshore financial centres, credible privacy oversight is treated as a condition of remaining an acceptable counterparty for international business.
Jamaica's timeline slips again

Jamaica illustrates how difficult implementation has proven. The Data Protection Act was passed in 2020, and the Office of the Information Commissioner, led by Information Commissioner Celia Barclay, has been building out registration and enforcement machinery since. Full enforcement, however, has now been pushed toward 2028, a further delay. The registration process for data controllers and processors was suspended on December 1, 2025, and is expected to resume toward the end of September 2026 once payment and systems upgrades are complete.

The Commissioner's office has been candid about capacity. It has described being constrained by human resource challenges affecting its ability to attract, recruit and retain suitable staff, with additional posts approved in late 2025 to expand its interim structure. Crucially, officials have stressed that organisations handling personal data remain legally obligated to comply even while registration is paused, a message businesses cannot afford to misread as a reprieve.
Trinidad and Tobago's unfinished statute

Trinidad and Tobago remains the most conspicuous laggard among the larger economies. Its Data Protection Act dates to 2011, but only a portion of the legislation was ever proclaimed, leaving the core operative provisions dormant. Recruitment activity for an Office of the Information Commissioner advanced during 2025, and legal commentators continue to identify the urgent need for a modernised statute aligned with contemporary standards.
The compliance and cross-border question

For Caribbean banks, fintechs and regional businesses, the practical challenge is the patchwork itself. An institution operating across Kingston, Bridgetown, Hamilton and George Town must reconcile several regimes with different registration duties, breach-notification rules and restrictions on moving data across borders. Compliance now demands data mapping, appointed privacy officers, vendor contracts and audit trails, all of which carry recurring cost.

Cross-border transfer is the sharpest pressure point. Regional financial institutions routinely route processing through overseas cloud providers and correspondent banks, and each new regime asks fresh questions about the legal basis for those flows. As commissioners in the more advanced jurisdictions gain enforcement teeth, the reputational and financial exposure of getting it wrong rises. The strategic lesson for the region is that privacy compliance has quietly become part of the cost of doing cross-border business in the Caribbean.

sources: Jamaica Gleaner, 'Data defence delay', July 30, 2026; Office of the Information Commissioner (Jamaica); Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Bermuda (PrivCom), Guide to PIPA; Appleby and Walkers, Bermuda PIPA guidance 2025; Cayman Islands Ombudsman, Data Protection; Government of Barbados, Data Protection Commission; Parliament of Trinidad and Tobago, Data Protection Act 2011; DLA Piper Data Protection Laws of the World

headline: Caribbean nurses depart as region races to keep its wards staffed
stand: As wealthy economies recruit ever harder, CARICOM and PAHO are building a managed-migration architecture to stem a workforce drain that threatens patient care.

blocks.x: The nurse who trains in Kingston, Bridgetown or St George's is increasingly likely to spend her career in London, Toronto or Miami. That reality, long familiar across the region, has hardened into a strategic emergency for Caribbean health systems, and in 2025 and 2026 it moved to the centre of the CARICOM and Pan American Health Organization agenda.
A drain measured in specialists

The numbers from Jamaica illustrate the pressure. The Ministry of Health and Wellness estimates the island loses roughly 500 specialist nurses each year to migration, and in 2024 the Nursing Council of Jamaica received more than 1,140 verification requests from foreign employers seeking to confirm Jamaican nursing credentials, a leading indicator of departures to come. Officials say vacancy rates exceed 40% in some facilities, with the sharpest gaps in critical care, emergency medicine and neonatology.

The pull is structural. In its State of the World's Nursing 2025 report, the World Health Organization noted that roughly one in seven nurses globally works outside the country of birth, a share that runs far higher for small island states that cannot match the salaries of ageing high-income economies.
The regional shortfall ahead

PAHO frames the recruitment as part of a wider crisis. At the International Forum on Human Resources for Health, held in Brasilia from July 23 to 25, 2025, the organization estimated that Latin America and the Caribbean could face a shortage of between 600,000 and 2 million health professionals by 2030. PAHO Director Dr Jarbas Barbosa said rising migration of health professionals places additional pressure on systems and worsens structural gaps and working conditions.

At the Regional Nursing Body's 52nd annual meeting in Barbados on August 12, 2025, Barbados Health Minister Dr Jerome Walcott described nursing as being at a critical crossroad, noting that smaller developing states cannot compete with wealthier nations on pay. Grenada's Chief Nursing Officer Nester Edwards, the body's chair, warned of a perennial shortage of nurses and midwives coupled with high attrition.
Building a managed-migration architecture

Rather than resist departures outright, the region is reviving and modernising a managed-migration approach it has advocated for decades: training more nurses than it needs, engaging the diaspora, and pressing destination countries toward ethical recruitment under the WHO Global Code of Practice. In Brasilia, 18 health ministries agreed to develop a joint roadmap for coordinated, ethical mobility.

That work advanced at the Tenth Meeting of the Human Resources for Health Caribbean Commission on June 17, 2026, convened by PAHO and the CARICOM Secretariat and now chaired by Guyana's Dr Asha Kisoon. The Commission endorsed a Human Resources for Resilient Health Systems Caribbean Roadmap 2025 to 2030, a Caribbean Action Plan on Migration and Mobility of Health Workers, and a Regional Nursing Body Strategic Plan Framework running to 2035.

National governments are testing their own levers. In January 2026, Jamaican Health Minister Dr Christopher Tufton issued a public appeal for diaspora specialist nurses to return home, offering relocation support and allowances across fields from oncology to mental health.
